chapters.summary: Council staff opens the joint hearing, asks attendees to silence phones, and explains how to fill out appearance cards. Staff states that no one may approach the dais and invites the chair to begin.
chapters.title: Sergeant at Arms gives hearing instructions and appearance card procedure

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Hello there, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Welcome to today's New York City Council hearing for the Committee on Economic Development and Small Business.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: At this time, please silence all phones.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If you wish to speak in today's hearing, please fill out an appearance card with one of the sergeants.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Moving forward, no one is to approach the dais.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Chair, you may begin.

chapters.summary: Virginia Maloney welcomes attendees to the joint hearing with the Committee on Small Business and introduces co-chair Shanel Thomas-Henry. She states the hearing will assess the economic impact of the 2026 FIFA World Cup.
chapters.title: Chair Maloney opens joint Economic Development and Small Business hearing on 2026 FIFA World Cup

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: All right, good afternoon and welcome to this joint hearing of the New York City Council's Committee on Economic Development and the Committee on Small Business.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Today is Wednesday, September 30th.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: My name is Virginia Maloney and I have the privilege of serving as chair of the Committee on Economic Development and I am so pleased to be joined by my co-chair, Councilmember Chanel Thomas-Henry, who chairs the Committee on Small Business.

chapters.summary: Maloney recalls prior oversight and legislation on World Cup preparations, bathroom access, event calendaring, small business maps, and cultural passports. She says today is a look back at what the city's investment produced and who benefited.
chapters.title: Maloney frames hearing as look back at World Cup spending and benefits

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Today, we are assessing the economic impact of the 2026 FIFA World Cup.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: This committee held an oversight hearing on the city's preparations in February, a hearing on World Cup legislation in April, and we passed three bills on bathroom access, on

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: events calendaring and a small business map, and a cultural passport program.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Today is a look back about what the city's investment actually produced, who benefited, and what the city should do differently the next time an event of this scale comes around.

chapters.summary: Maloney notes free fan events in all five boroughs, 30,000 people watching the final in Central Park, and New Jersey Transit moving over 300,000 passengers across eight matches. She says there is a lot to celebrate.
chapters.title: Maloney highlights World Cup successes: free fan events and transit

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: First, we'd like to discuss the World Cup successes, what worked well, and what should become part of a long-term playbook for the city of New York.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: We held free fan events in all five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: 30,000 people watched the final on the Great Lawn in Central Park.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And New Jersey Transit, for the most part, moved more than 300,000 passengers across the eight matches at MetLife Stadium.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So there is a lot to celebrate.

chapters.summary: Maloney says Council Finance analysis shows hosting the World Cup cost the city more than it brought in. She argues taxpayers may have subsidized a payday for FIFA and says the city still lacks a meaningful account of where money went.
chapters.title: Maloney raises return-on-investment concerns and missing spending details

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Second, we'd like to understand the return on investment here.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: The Council's Finance Division has an analysis showing that hosting the World Cup cost the city more than it brought in.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: There were some projections released earlier today in a press release, and we'd like to understand the...

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: True return on investment from these various sources and whether or not this was a net cost to the city.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Put simply, New York City taxpayers might have helped subsidize a tremendous payday for FIFA, and we'll be digging in more onto that with a resolution that my council member colleague will present.

chapters.summary: Maloney says EDC passed $20 million to the host committee and the administration added $15 million, with $9 million for fan zones. She questions the host committee's $3.5 billion regional impact figure and its methodology.
chapters.title: Maloney details city funding pass-through and host committee impact claims

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So we still also don't have a meaningful account of where exactly all of the money went.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: In February, EDC told us that it had passed $20 million through to the host committee and committed to sharing a breakdown of how that money was spent along with the agreement to the host committee.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So we're hoping to get more specifics on the agreement.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: We did receive a breakdown of the additional $15 million that the Madamian administration added.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Of that $15 million, $9 million was allocated to fan zones, and we want to understand how that was distributed across all five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: In August, the host committee reported around $3.5 billion in regional economic impact.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: That number covers both New York and New Jersey together.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So we're trying to understand the host committee's methodology.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: of what specifically happened in New York.

chapters.summary: Maloney notes the World Cup occurred during peak tourist season and may have displaced regular visitors. She introduces Resolution 655 calling on FIFA to pay New York City the promised $1 million legacy contribution.
chapters.title: Maloney questions displacement and introduces FIFA legacy contribution resolution

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: The World Cup fell during peak tourist season, so many World Cup visitors simply may have taken the place of tourists who could have come anyway.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So we want to better understand, again, the methodology.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Chair Thomas Henry and I have introduced Resolution No.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: 655, which calls on FIFA.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: To pay New Yorkers in New York City the one million legacy contribution that was promised for hosting the cup.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I'll leave it to Chanel Thomas-Henry, my councilwoman co-chair, to speak to that resolution.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And finally, in closing, this hearing is as much about the next event as it is the last one.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: In July 2028, Queens is set to host nine Olympic soccer matches.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: The lessons of the World Cup this summer should shape how the city approaches that event and everyone like it.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: We need commitments from event organizers in writing before committing public money, and we need to account publicly for every dollar that passes through to a third party.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: The 2028 Olympics are less than two years away, and that planning needs to start now.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: We want to hear from the administration today about what the city spent, what New Yorkers got for that money, and how the city plans to carry those lessons forward.

chapters.summary: Maloney recognizes Economic Development Committee staff including Alex Polinoff, William Hongnash, and Spencer Kuhn. She then turns the floor over to co-chair Shanel Thomas-Henry.
chapters.title: Maloney thanks committee staff and turns to co-chair Thomas-Henry

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Before I pass to my colleague, I want to recognize the Economic Development Committee staff for their work in preparing for today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you to Senior Counsel Alex Polinoff, Senior Policy Analyst William Hongnash,

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And financial analyst Spencer Kuhn.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I will now turn the floor over to my co-chair.

chapters.summary: Shanel Thomas-Henry introduces herself as chair of the Committee on Small Business and thanks attendees. She says the administration announced an estimated $2 billion in economic activity for New York City.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry opens Small Business Committee remarks on World Cup benefits

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Maloney.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I am Councilmember Chanel Thomas-Henry, Chair of the Committee on Small Business.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you for joining us for today's joint hearing.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry says headline economic activity does not show who benefited. She asks whether restaurant owners in Corona, small businesses in the Bronx, Brooklyn, Staten Island, and Southeast Queens saw new customers.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry questions whether small businesses felt the $2 billion impact

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Today, the administration announced that the World Cup generated an estimated $2 billion in economic activity for New York City.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: That is significant, and it gives us an important starting point for today's conversation.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: But in a city as large as New York, headline economic activity alone does not tell us who actually benefited from it.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: The question before us today is, did New Yorkers feel it?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Did the restaurant owner in Corona see new customers come through their doors?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Did the small business in the Bronx, Brooklyn, Staten Island, or Southeast Queens get a piece of that $2 billion?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And after the crowds went home, did those businesses walk away stronger than they were before?

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry quotes Mayor Mamdani saying the World Cup belonged to deli owners, cab drivers, and line cooks. She says it is clear what New Yorkers did for the World Cup and asks what the World Cup did for New Yorkers.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry contrasts what New Yorkers did for World Cup with what they received

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Mayor Momdani said today that the World Cup belonged to the deli owners, cab drivers, and line cooks who welcomed the world to New York.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I agree that those New Yorkers helped make this tournament possible.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: It's clear what New Yorkers did for the World Cup.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Today, we want to understand what the World Cup did for New Yorkers.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry says the 2026 World Cup was the largest in tournament history, with more than one million people coming to the New York-New Jersey region. She says small businesses are still holding their breath while the administration celebrates.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry notes record World Cup scale and small business uncertainty

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: The World Cup 2026 was the largest of the tournament's existence.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: More than one million people came to the New York, New Jersey region.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: New York welcomed visitors, supported transportation and public safety, hosted fan events, and helped create the experience that allowed this global event to succeed.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: But while this admin celebrates, small businesses across the city are still holding their breath.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And that is why a headline number cannot be the end of this conversation.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry says the city must look beyond aggregate economic activity to see where it occurred, which industries benefited, and which neighborhoods saw foot traffic. She asks how many local businesses participated and whether opportunities were equitably distributed.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry calls for neighborhood-level and industry-level impact data

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: We must look beyond aggregate economic activity and ask where that activity occurred.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Which industries benefited?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Which neighborhoods saw increased foot traffic?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: How many local businesses participated, and whether the opportunities were equitably distributed across all five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Because the goal cannot simply be to hope that economic activity trickles into our neighborhoods.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry says the city must build infrastructure to intentionally direct opportunities to neighborhoods. She calls for earlier coordination with BIDs, chambers, vendors, restaurants, and retailers, and highlights Resolution 655 on FIFA's $1 million legacy contribution.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry urges coordinated playbook and FIFA legacy contribution

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: We have to build the infrastructure that intentionally directs opportunities there.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: That means coordinating earlier with bids, chambers, merchant associations, street vendors, restaurants, and retailers so businesses know what is coming and how they can participate.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And it means removing barriers and creating clear pathways for businesses across all five boroughs to turn major events into real lasting economic activity.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: That also includes examining the commitments made to our city.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Resolution 655, which I sponsor, calls on FIFA to provide New York City with the $1 million legacy contribution associated with hosting the tournament that they promised.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Together, we are demanding New York gets what it was promised and better prepares us for what's ahead.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry says the joint hearing should help build a coordinated playbook for future major events so small businesses and working people benefit from day one. She thanks Central Staff and her staff, then acknowledges attending council colleagues.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry calls for playbook for future events and thanks staff

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: That's why I'm proud to hold this joint hearing to determine how the city can build a coordinated playbook for future major events so that when New York

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: welcomes the world, our small businesses and working people are positioned from day one to benefit from it.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I look forward to hearing from the administration today about the economic impact of the tournament.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I want to thank Tyler Walls and Rebecca Barilla from Central Staff for their work putting this hearing together, as well as my staff,

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Franklin Richards, Sierra Smith, and Elise Francisco, and everyone working behind the scenes to make today's hearing possible.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: At this time, I want to acknowledge that we are joined by our council colleagues, Councilmember Marano, Councilmembers Brooks-Powers, Councilmember Salam, and Councilmember Santos-Wilson.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And Council Member Banks.

chapters.summary: Chair Maloney turns to committee counsel Alex Polanoff. Polanoff asks all administration witnesses to raise their right hands and swear or affirm to tell the truth.
chapters.title: Committee counsel administers oath to administration witnesses

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: We'll now turn to committee counsel to administer the oath.

utterances.speaker: Alex Polanoff
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairs.

utterances.speaker: Alex Polanoff
utterances.text: Alex Polanoff, Committee Counsel.

utterances.speaker: Alex Polanoff
utterances.text: Will all members of the administration testifying today please raise your right hands?

utterances.speaker: Alex Polanoff
utterances.text: Do you swear or affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth in your testimony today, and to respond honestly to Councilmember questions?

utterances.speaker: Alex Polanoff
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Alex Polanoff
utterances.text: You may begin when ready.

chapters.summary: Maya Honda introduces herself as World Cup czar and greets the chairs and committee members. She briefly acknowledges the New York Liberty's championship before turning to soccer.
chapters.title: World Cup Czar Maya Honda begins administration testimony

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: Perfect.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Maloney, Chair Thomas Henry, and members of the committees.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And thank you for the opportunity to speak with City Council today.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: My name is Maya Honda, World Cup czar.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: Even though basketball is not my purview, I would be remiss if we did not acknowledge the historic performance of the New York Liberty last night.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: Incredible sweep of the links, so just want to shout them out for that.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And then move on to soccer.

chapters.summary: Honda says the tournament brought historic opportunities and complex challenges. She says Mayor Mamdani wanted every New Yorker to participate, the city to stay safe and moving, and bars, restaurants, and businesses in all five boroughs to benefit.
chapters.title: Honda outlines World Cup goals: access, safety, and small business benefits

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: So this summer, we welcomed more than 1 million people from around the world for the 2026 FIFA World Cup.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: The tournament not only brought historic opportunities for our city, but intricate and complex challenges as well.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: Mayor Momdani was clear from the outset.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: We had to make sure that every New Yorker could be a part of the celebration.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: We had to keep our city safe and our streets moving.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And we had to make sure that bars, restaurants, and business from across all five boroughs benefited from the World Cup.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: Thanks to the tireless preparation of our city agencies and the dedication of New Yorkers both inside and outside of city government, this tournament was a success on all three fronts.

chapters.summary: Honda says the World Cup added more than $3.5 billion to the regional economy and about $2 billion in New York City economic activity. She cites 16% higher sports bar foot traffic, over $1 billion in additional hotel revenue, and more than 12,000 jobs supported.
chapters.title: Honda reports $3.5B regional and $2B NYC economic impact

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: The World Cup added more than $3.5 billion to our regional economy, to our hotels, small businesses, and commercial corridors.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: Not only is that real money in the pockets of business owners and workers, it's $200 million more than initially projected.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: Within New York City, the tournament generated approximately $2 billion in economic activity, more than half of the total regional impact and more than two-thirds of all direct visitor spending.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: The numbers are clear.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: Major international events can deliver for New York City's economy.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: They can deliver for our sports bars, where foot traffic increased by 16% year over year throughout the tournament.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: They can deliver for our hotels, who saw over a billion dollars in additional revenue thanks to the World Cup.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And they can deliver for workers with more than 12,000 jobs supported by visitor and operational spending from the tournament.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: This explosion in economic activity was not limited to any single sector.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: Hospitality, food service, retail, and tourism all benefited from this summer.

chapters.summary: Honda says the success was not guaranteed and resulted from administration efforts to engage businesses and host events. She cites more than 100 free watch parties, 1,000 affordable tickets, and soccer fields open 24-7 in every borough.
chapters.title: Honda details city programs: watch parties, tickets, 24-7 soccer fields

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: But I want to be clear.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: The success of this tournament and the benefits that it brought to New Yorkers were not guaranteed.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: They were the direct result of the Mamdani administration's efforts to engage businesses of all kind, drive foot traffic to every borough, and host events for every New Yorker.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: To make sure that New Yorkers could be a part of this historic tournament, we hosted more than 100 free watch parties in our parks, plazas, and public spaces.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: We secured 1,000 affordable tickets to World Cup matches for New Yorkers and kept soccer fields in every borough open 24-7 to give people a place to play long after the sun had set.

chapters.summary: Honda says the city expanded ferry service and launched a midtown transportation plan with dedicated bus and shuttle corridors. She also highlights a $26 meal deal, cultural passport program, and a small business toolkit reaching more than 56,000 New Yorkers.
chapters.title: Honda describes transportation, meal deal, and small business toolkit

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: To keep our city safe and moving, we brought together agencies across multiple levels of city government, expanded ferry service, and launched a midtown transportation plan with dedicated bus and shuttle corridors.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: To drive traffic to commercial quarters,

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: corridors across the city, we launched a $26 meal deal for our restaurants, a cultural passport program for cultural organizations and small businesses and business districts, and a small business toolkit that reached more than 56,000 New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: From breweries on Staten Island to museums in Queens to watch parties in the Bronx, we brought businesses and organizations across the city together to take part in the celebration.

chapters.summary: Honda says the mayor wanted a legacy beyond the final whistle. She describes EDC's Choose NYC Summit with 350 attendees from 150 businesses and 34 countries, plus permanent projects like a bus lane near LaGuardia and a Brooklyn Bridge bike connection.
chapters.title: Honda highlights legacy efforts and permanent public space projects

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: But the mayor's mandate was clear.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: We needed to build a legacy that lasted beyond the final whistle.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: That's why the city's Economic Development Corporation leveraged the global attention surrounding the event to connect businesses with city leadership, highlight opportunities for investment and expansion, and showcase New York City as a destination for growth and innovation.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: During the tournament, NYC EDC hosted its annual Choose NYC Summit, bringing together more than 350 attendees representing 150 businesses from 34 countries.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: EDC also organized site visits and tours across multiple neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And New York City Tourism welcomed guests, encouraged them to explore the breadth of the city, and ultimately created return visitors.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: Our city launched projects to permanently transform public spaces, like a new bus lane near LaGuardia Airport, a dedicated bike and pedestrian connection near the Brooklyn Bridge, and much more.

chapters.summary: Honda says the outcomes prove major events can translate into real economic impacts across the five boroughs. She says the city must take an active role in supporting local businesses and coordinating future events, and closes with memories of fans watching Argentina's comebacks and Central Park finals.
chapters.title: Honda concludes with lessons on coordination and World Cup memories

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: Taken together, these outcomes prove that major international sporting events like the World Cup can translate into real economic impacts for New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: That we can not only welcome visitors from around the world, but direct their attention, investment, and spending toward businesses and neighborhoods across the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: But these findings also make it clear that it's not simply enough that it's not simply enough.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: for cities to open up their doors to these events.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: City governments must take an active role in supporting local businesses, attracting investment, driving foot traffic to commercial corridors, and ensuring that major events are accessible to working people.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: These lessons of coordination must be front and center as New York City continues to compete for and host international events.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: Ultimately, though, we know that when New Yorkers remember the World Cup, they won't remember good economic statistics or the hard data of dollar figures.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: They will remember crowding into bars to watch Argentina maneuver two breathtaking comebacks.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: They will remember riding World Cup-branded trains and ferries across the five boroughs to collect commemorative cups and stamps.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: They'll remember laying a blanket down on the great lawn of Central Park to watch the finals match, then instantly standing back up again to cheer on their team.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: That is what this tournament was ultimately about.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: As we look ahead to future international events and opportunities, we will continue to build on the lessons learned from the World Cup, using data and experience to strengthen our approach and maximize benefits to New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: I look forward to answering your questions.

chapters.summary: Nancy Mamana introduces herself as chief marketing officer for New York City Tourism and Conventions. She thanks the committees and says she will share results of tourism marketing around the World Cup.
chapters.title: NYC Tourism CMO Nancy Mamana begins testimony

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Council Chair Maloney, Council Chair Thomas Henry, and members of the Economic Development and Small Business Committees.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: I'm Nancy Mamana, Chief Marketing Officer for New York City Tourism and Conventions.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to share the results of our work surrounding the World Cup and specifically how the city's investment in tourism marketing helped translate this extraordinary global event into economic activity across all five boroughs.

chapters.summary: Mamana says NYC Tourism is the city's official destination marketing organization and represents more than 1,600 member businesses. She says tourism supports nearly 400,000 workers, with nearly 80% living outside Manhattan and Brooklyn.
chapters.title: Mamana describes NYC Tourism mission and workforce reach

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: New York City Tourism and Conventions is the city's official destination marketing organization and convention and visitors bureau, and our role is to promote New York City to travelers around the world, encourage visitation, and help visitors discover more of the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Our mission is to maximize inbound travel and tourism opportunities in support of equitable economic prosperity for local businesses throughout the city.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: New York City Tourism represents more than 1,600 member businesses and is governed by an 80-member board of directors representing the diversity of New York City's businesses.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Tourism supports nearly 400,000 workers across the city, which is roughly 10% of the city's workforce.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Nearly 80% of those workers live outside of Manhattan and Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx, and Staten Island.

chapters.summary: Mamana says the World Cup was never just about filling the stadium and that tourism aimed to spread impact beyond it. She describes a $4.5 million investment in advertising, social media, NBC and Telemundo partnerships, borough grants, and small business toolkits.
chapters.title: Mamana outlines $4.5M tourism investment and borough outreach

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: For us, the World Cup was never just about filling the stadium.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Our responsibility was to make sure the impact of visitation extended way beyond the stadium and into New York City businesses, neighborhoods, and communities.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: So as a result of that, we approached the World Cup with two clear goals.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: First, we wanted to leverage the global appeal of the World Cup to drive visitation and spending to businesses across all five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Secondly, we wanted to create a joyous, welcoming citywide experience that generated lasting exposure for the city.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Our $4.5 million investment in tourism for the World Cup allowed us to do just that through outdoor and digital advertising, our social media content, partnerships with major media outlets like NBC and Telemundo,

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: and programs that connected visitors directly with businesses and experiences across all five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: As you have heard from Maya, the economic impact of the World Cup was substantial.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: We created direct pathways to local businesses and neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: We funded borough grants delivered in partnership with borough presidents.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: We worked with NYU to distribute 13,000 toolkits to small businesses throughout the city with the help of our bids chambers and SBS, which gave local businesses ready-to-use World Cup marketing assets, messaging, and guidance.

chapters.summary: Mamana says NYC Tourism launched an AI-enabled chatbot in 50 languages and the Five Borough Winner Special with $26 food and drink specials. She says 133,000 commemorative cups were distributed to almost 1,000 food and beverage businesses across the boroughs.
chapters.title: Mamana details Five Borough Winner Special and multilingual chatbot

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: We implemented an AI-enabled chatbot, which connected visitors directly to World Cup information and recommendations in 50 languages.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: We designed and executed the Five Borough Winner Special, a program offering $26 food and drink specials and commemorative cups, one for each borough.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: 133,000 were distributed to almost 1,000 local food and beverage businesses, 569 in Manhattan, 182 in Brooklyn, 152 in Queens, 33 in the Bronx, and 22 on Staten Island.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: In a recent survey, which is still ongoing, 8 in 10 local...

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Business participants said they were satisfied with the program, and 9 and 10 said they would participate in a similar promotion again.

chapters.summary: Mamana says the World Cup calendar featured more than 1,700 events, 17 times the city's previous highest-performing calendar. She says the digital campaign influenced about 164,000 visitors and generated an estimated $147 million in direct visitor spending.
chapters.title: Mamana reports campaign influenced 164,000 visitors and $147M spend

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Our World Cup calendar featured more than 1,700 events, offers, and borough-based experiences.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: This is 17 times the number included in our highest-performing event calendar of the past three years, which was for the city's 400th.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: And our marketing produced measurable results.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: We were able to share more of this data in part because we were also funded to include measurement of our digital initiatives using third-party tools.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Specifically, we partnered with Tourism Economics to measure the $1 million portion, which was a programmatic digital media buy of the World Campaign.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: This type of campaign uses technology to buy digital ads across several sites, focusing on people with very specific behavior.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: In this case, we focused on those who showed intent to travel to New York City this summer and those who typically travel for big sporting events.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: This allows us to see how many people saw our ads and then arrived in the city.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Our campaign influenced approximately 164,000 visitors who would not have otherwise visited without seeing that advertising.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Of those, 44% went to Brooklyn, 40% to Queens, 49% to Manhattan, 13% to Staten Island, and 24% to the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: We also know the campaign generated an estimated $147 million in direct visitor spend and $213 million in total economic impact.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Ultimately, we saw that for every $1 spent on this digital advertising,

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Those visitors spent $147 in New York City.

chapters.summary: Mamana says Visa data showed incremental visitor spending increased 19% in Brooklyn and 6% in Queens, with hotel demand rising outside Manhattan. She also describes the Where the World Comes to Play campaign generating more than 1.2 billion impressions.
chapters.title: Mamana cites borough visitor spending and campaign impressions

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: We also saw broader evidence that the visitor activity extended beyond Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Incremental visitor spending increased 19% in Brooklyn and 6% in Queens, according to Visa credit card spending data.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Hotel demand increased in Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx, and Staten Island, and nearly 400 businesses outside of Manhattan participated in the Five Borough Winter Special, as mentioned earlier, which illustrates significant borough dispersion.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: These results demonstrate that our World Cup marketing investment helped broaden the event's economic footprint and brought measurable visitor activity into communities across the city.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Secondly, in the goal of creating a joyous, welcoming citywide experience, in working with the mayor's office, we also deployed the unified Where the World Comes to Play campaign throughout the city.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: This manifested in billboards, airport signage, subway cards, bus signage, along with bus shelters and link screens throughout the city, which generated more than 1.2 billion impressions.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: And our NBC and Telemundo partnership generated about 29 million television impressions.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Our World Cup website content generated more than 1.3 million page views, which is 13 times higher than our historically highest performing campaigns, connecting consumers to businesses, neighborhoods, events, and attractions throughout New York City.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Online conversation about New York City, which we track through a system called Meltwater, which is a social media and press tracking platform, became markedly more positive during the World Cup.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: In July, positive traveler sentiment reached its highest level of the year, which was about 11 percentage points above the pre-World Cup average.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: This increase suggests that the World Cup period coincided with a significant lift in positive conversation about the city.

chapters.summary: Mamana says the World Cup showed what New York can achieve with coordinated citywide effort. She argues sustained destination marketing can turn global attention into visitation and economic opportunity across all five boroughs.
chapters.title: Mamana concludes tourism investment yielded citywide impact

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: The World Cup demonstrated what New York City can achieve when a global moment is matched by a coordinated citywide effort.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Thanks to our partners at the mayor's office, council, borough presidents, Maya Handa, EDC, SBS, the bids and all the chambers, and sustained investment in tourism marketing that turns global attention into visitation and economic impact.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: We saw international visitor spending grow across multiple boroughs, hotel demand rise beyond Manhattan, engagement increase citywide, hundreds of local businesses participating, and a global campaign that reached millions with a clear message, New York City welcomes the world.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: The additional 4.5 investment allowed us to reach potential visitors at a scale we otherwise could not have achieved, particularly through outdoor and programmatic digital advertising.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Our programs then gave those audiences concrete reasons to explore, engage, and spend throughout New York City.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: The city's investment in tourism during the World Cup is an example of how tourism yields significant impact across the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: With sustained investment in destination marketing, New York City can continue to compete for high-spending visitors from around the world who explore every borough, turning that visitation into economic opportunity throughout the city.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Thank you again for...

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: for the opportunity to testify, and I look forward to answering your questions.

chapters.summary: Maloney thanks the panel and notes she has the full set of World Cup cups. She asks the panel to explain how the $2 billion, $1.2 billion direct spending, and 12,000 jobs figures were calculated.
chapters.title: Maloney asks panel to explain World Cup economic impact methodology

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Well, thank you so much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And I forgot to bring my World Cup cups, but I have the full set.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And have to commend you on the world comes to play marketing slogan, which I think we all really appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you also for sharing a lot of the numbers, and it's clear there was a substantial economic impact.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I heard $2 billion, 1.2 in direct spending, and roughly 12K jobs created.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And wanted to open to the panel to just dig in a bit more to the methodology that was used there and if you could explain how we came to those numbers.

chapters.summary: Justin Kreamer of NYC EDC says Tourism Economics conducted the studies and is a globally renowned tourism analysis firm. He explains the bottom-up approach using out-of-region match attendees and official fan zone visitors.
chapters.title: Justin Kreamer explains Tourism Economics direct visitor spending model

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Yep, I can jump in.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Justin Kramer with the New York City Economic Development Corporation.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So I'll start by saying both studies were done by Tourism Economics.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Tourism Economics is a globally renowned organization that does specifically tourism economic analysis.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: It's the same organization that, for example, London used when they were reviewing their 2012 Olympics, amongst other...

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Recent hosts of the World Cup across the city have also used them as well.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So very reputable organization.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: The way that the numbers came to pass, and I'll kind of break it out into pieces here.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So it starts off with identifying what is the direct spending.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So the direct spending is broken up into two different parts.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: The first part of it is direct spending from visitors to New York City.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And the way that number is calculated is it specifically looks at two different groups.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: It takes kind of a bottom-up approach.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So the first group is how many people attended a match from outside of the region.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And so that number is...

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: There was 645,000 people who attended the eight matches.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Of that number, 78% came from outside of the New York City region.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So that is 508,000 people.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: On top of that, it looks at who attended the official World Cup band zones and related events.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Through that, on top of it, there was another 626,000 people from outside of the region who came to New York.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So this report specifically looks at visitors to New York City, not New York City residents spending, to be clear.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So that's the...

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: I'm laughing because last time I did this, I was too quiet, so I will try to speak louder.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: I feel like I'm eating the microphone now, but this is close to me.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So that's how the visitor numbers were calculated.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Then that information is put into a model that the organization has that looks at typical visitor spending, actual numbers of spending at the MetLife Stadium, et cetera,

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: and by sector calculates an estimated amount of money that each visitor would spend in New York City.

chapters.summary: Kreamer says operational spending includes host committee funds from federal, state, municipal, and donor sources. He explains indirect spending through a restaurant buying more fish and induced spending through workers spending extra wages in their neighborhoods.
chapters.title: Kreamer breaks down operational, indirect, and induced spending

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: The second part of the equation is operational spending.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And so that is money that the host committee spent to actually execute on the World Cup happening here in the region.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And so that is money that went in from the federal government, money that went in from the state, money came in from various municipalities, donors that were part of fundraising efforts that the host committee made.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And so that collective amount is the amount of operational spending.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So you take both the visitor spending, you take the...

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Operational spending.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And that's where you get the, for New York City specifically, the $1.2 billion in direct spending.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Now, the economic impact of those dollars and those visitors don't stop with direct spending.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: There are some knock-on effects as well, specifically.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Indirect spending and also induced spending.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So to give an example of indirect spending, if I own a restaurant in Brooklyn and I need to buy more fish, let's say,

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: to serve the additional customers who are coming in because of the World Cup, that's the indirect spending as a result of the visitor spending coming into the city, if that makes sense.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So that is indirect spending.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And then the induced spending is sticking with the analogy of the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: If a waiter, let's say, works at the restaurant and they've picked up an extra shift or they get additional tips or whatever it may be, that extra money gets recycled into the city's economy as well.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So they're going to go back to their neighborhood and they're going to spend that money at their local bodega.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: They're going to spend it maybe on the rent.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: They're going to spend it on other things.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So there is an analysis that's done that calculates roughly how much that is, both for indirect and for induced.

chapters.summary: Kreamer says $1.2 billion in direct spending plus about $700 million in indirect and induced effects yields the $2 billion figure. He says the 12,100 jobs are supported jobs, not necessarily new jobs, and the analysis cannot distinguish temporary from permanent.
chapters.title: Kreamer explains $2B total and 12,100 jobs supported

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And so that number, again, for New York City specifically, is about $700,000 added on top of the direct spending.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So 1.2, sorry, 1.3 plus $700,000 is how we.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: We got to the $2 billion number.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And the same process works out for the regional numbers that you all have cited as well before, which was the regionals.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: It was $1.9 billion in direct spending and $3.5 billion in overall economic impact.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: I can also answer the question on the job supported as well, I believe that was part of it.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Yeah, cool.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I'm learning a lot.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: I feel like I'm a professor slowly breaking down by step by step.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So the way that the job supported was calculated is by sector.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: They track each dollar that is spent can be attributed to supporting a job or multiple jobs within that sector.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And so based off that total spending broken up by the sectors, it then multiplies that dollar by the number of jobs that dollar supported.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And that's how the 12,100 jobs was calculated.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And to be clear, those aren't new jobs.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Those are jobs that are supported.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: There may be some new jobs that were in there, seasonal jobs that came in, full-time jobs, but you can't distinguish that through the analysis.

chapters.summary: Maloney asks if the jobs were temporary over the World Cup period or had long-term impact. Kreamer says the Tourism Economics analysis does not disaggregate the information to that level.
chapters.title: Maloney asks whether supported jobs were temporary

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So on the jobs, were those just temporary over the period, or how are you thinking about the long-term?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: term impact.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Yeah, for the analysis that was done by Tourism Economics, it doesn't disaggregate the information to that level.

chapters.summary: Maloney asks what city tax revenue the $2 billion economic impact generated, noting the city investment was roughly $90 million. Maya Honda says the event stretched across agencies, government levels, and fiscal years, and the city is still evaluating costs and projected tax revenue.
chapters.title: Maloney asks about city tax revenue return on $90M investment

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So all up, I guess, what do you expect the city tax revenue generated by that $2 billion economic impact to be?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And as a refresher, while we're talking about that, the city investment was roughly $90 million, I believe.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So just trying to get at what the return was if we got our money back, so to say.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: So this was an event that stretched across multiple agencies, multiple levels of government, and multiple fiscal years.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: So we're still evaluating both the total cost of the event as well as the projected tax revenue.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: What we do know from today's analysis is that the World Cup brought around $2 billion to New York City's economy, supported 12,000 jobs, and reached across all five boroughs.

chapters.summary: Maloney asks how the completed analysis compares to earlier projections. Kreamer says the initial regional projection was $3.3 billion and the post-event regional result was $3.5 billion, a $200 million increase, but there was no pre-event New York City-specific baseline.
chapters.title: Kreamer compares regional projections to post-World Cup results

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: On the, I guess you've now completed this analysis, how does it compare to what the projections were?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Where were you on point?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Where were projections a bit off?

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So to make one, thank you for the question, to distinguish one thing.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So the initial projections that you all may remember, which was regionally $3.3 billion, that was for the region.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: That was also done by tourism economics.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So the same company?

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: The same company, correct, that did both.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: post-World Cup, the city and the region.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: We intentionally chose the same organizations, so we have an apples-to-apples comparison.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: There was no pre-New York City-specific analysis done, so we only can look at the regional analysis, which, again, netted out to be $3.3 billion, and then the post-World Cup was $3.5 billion.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So as a region, we saw a bump or an increase of $200 million, which is positive.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: We can't break it down further than that because we have no baseline to compare it to for the city.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: But we do know that we did see a lift in a lot of numbers that show that there was people who came to the city, subway ridership up, NYC ferry ridership up.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: City bike ridership up, I think, 20%.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: I'll have to fact check myself here, but roughly 20% more international visitors using city bike versus the previous year.

chapters.summary: Maloney asks for the total number of out-of-state visitors and how many attended matches versus free events. Kreamer says there were about 1.134 million visitors, with 508,000 attending matches and 626,000 attending official World Cup events.
chapters.title: Maloney asks about visitor breakdown between matches and fan events

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: On the visitors, the total number of out-of-state visitors, if you could remind me.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Yeah, the total of visitors was roughly 1.1.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Let's see here.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: 1.134 million.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And do we have a sense of whether or not those visitors were actually attending the cup or going to the free events and how that shook out?

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Yeah, so the breakout was those who attended the matches, 508,000 people from outside the region attended the matches.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And then there was another 626,000 who attended events within the city that were official World Cup events.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So roughly 50-50.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: For those of us looking for simple numbers.

chapters.summary: Maloney asks whether the analysis accounts for opportunity costs from displacing regular summer tourists. Kreamer says Tourism Economics removed displacement from the $2 billion figure and notes some visitors may return later or be newly exposed to New York.
chapters.title: Kreamer says displacement was incorporated into economic analysis

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: One last question here on the opportunity cost.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So summer is a big tourism.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: It's period for New York City.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Does the analysis have or speak to the opportunity costs from displacing regular tourists for the FIFA-related ones?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: You could speak to that.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you for the question, and I meant to bring that up earlier.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So thank you.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: The analysis at Tourism Economics does take into consideration displacement from those who may have not come to New York City because of higher hotel costs or because they frankly didn't want to be in the city when there was an influx of more people being here.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And so that number was removed from the $2 billion number.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So it's already incorporated into it.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Keep in mind that also does not take into consideration that a lot of people were exposed to the World Cup, New York City through the World Cup, and so it may lead to new tourists coming.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And also folks who may have just delayed their trip and will still come to the city, just push it back by a few weeks.

chapters.summary: Honda says the original plan had FanFest in New Jersey, but the administration worked with the host committee to bring free FanFests to all five boroughs. Kreamer adds that New York City captured 70% of the region's $1.7 billion in visitor spending.
chapters.title: Honda and Kreamer discuss bringing FanFest to NYC and capturing visitor spending

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: Can I add briefly?

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: So initially when we took office, the plan had been for there to be, the games would be in New Jersey and the FanFest would be in New Jersey as well.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And so one of the things our administration did was work with the FIFA host committee to bring FanFest to the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And so the 600,000 number of people who came

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: from outside of this region to New York City for the World Cup.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: You know, they could have gone to New Jersey for the FanFest, and in the end, we had free FanFests across all five boroughs, which we feel really strongly did drive visitation and also spend across the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And that reminds me of a stat I meant to mention earlier.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: To Maya's point, the city did capture 70% of visitor spending in the region.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Relative to New Jersey?

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: To the whole region.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So the whole region experienced $1.7 billion in visitor spending, and we got 70% of that.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So clear majority.

chapters.summary: Maloney asks how much of the $2 billion impact came from higher prices due to demand rather than additional transactions. Kreamer says the model is an input-output model calibrated to New York City and did consider a bump in lodging prices.
chapters.title: Kreamer addresses whether impact came from higher prices or more transactions

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: You mentioned higher prices.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I'm curious if you have a sense of how much of that $2.7 billion

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Two billion economic impact is from higher prices due to more demand.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: For example, I think.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: that was true with hotel pricing or additional transactions.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So the model did take into consideration, well, I'll take a step back.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So the model is based off of something that's called a implant input output model.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And that model is a industry agreed upon

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: model that is calibrated to the New York City market.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And so based off the prices of goods or services, based off the different sectors, and so the report did take consideration a bump in prices for lodging.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: I'm happy to follow up with some more information on that.

chapters.summary: Maloney acknowledges Council Member Hanif and notes Council Member Riley was present earlier. She then passes questioning to co-chair Thomas-Henry.
chapters.title: Maloney acknowledges additional members and passes to co-chair

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I want to acknowledge that we were joined by Councilmember Hanif and that Councilmember Riley was here earlier.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And now I'll pass to my co-chair.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks whether the city knows the economic impact of New York City tourism during the same period in 2025. Nancy Mamana says she does not have that broken out but can follow up.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry asks for 2025 tourism economic impact comparison

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: My first question is, do we know the economic impact of New York City tourism the same period in 2025?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Do you mean total visitor spend?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Well, like, because we're comparing, we're saying the World Cup generated $2 billion in total economic impact and $1.2 billion in direct visitor spending.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Do you know those numbers for 2025?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: We can come back.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: We don't have a broken out in that way, but we can.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Just to get a better understanding of where we really net it from the World Cup.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry notes the World Cup overlapped with the 250th anniversary celebration and asks how much impact is attributable to each. Kreamer says Tourism Economics used out-of-market match attendees and official World Cup event attendees as the baseline.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry questions separating World Cup impact from 250th and Knicks events

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Second question, the World Cup and the 250th celebration overlapped.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Have you assessed how much of that economic impact can be attributed directly to the World Cup versus what can be attributed to the visitors we got for the 250th anniversary?

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Yeah, so the way that tourism economics went about trying to disaggregate that information as best as possible was, again, using as the baseline of the analysis of that

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: number of people who attended a World Cup game from out of the market and those who attended a World Cup affiliated event from outside the market.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And so that's the base that was used.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: If you were here for the Knicks parade specifically or anything else, that would not have been counted if you didn't go to the game or you didn't go to an official fan fest.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Good point.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I forgot about the Nixon five.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So I'm just curious, like, how do you separate that?

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: The way it's separated is identifying who specifically went to, like who came to New York City with the intent of watching a World Cup match.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Right, who bought a ticket from out of the market.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And so that is one portion of the equation.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And then the other portion of the equation is who showed up to a,

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: a authorizer, an official World Cup fan zone event.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And based off that information is how we get to determine that that person came to New York City for the World Cup specifically.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay, so what if I wanted to come and I celebrated the Knicks in five, came to the parade and said, oh, man, there's a fan fest in my neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I want to go and check that out.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I wasn't coming for the World Cup, but I came to celebrate the Knicks.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So are we counting what could have otherwise brought someone to the city as World Cup if they just happened to stumble upon World Cup activities?

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: I'd have to go look at the calendar, but from what I recall, the parade was kind of at the beginning of the World Cup and a war that overlapped with the fan zone events.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Or just in general.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I come to New York.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I want to come see a play.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: But I'm like, oh, my gosh, the World Cup.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And I may want to check something out.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So currently, right now, there's no way of us saying someone came specifically for World Cup.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And this is what you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: generated versus someone came just because this is New York City and then decided to partake in any World Cup activities.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So a lion's share of the analysis is based on people who came to New York City who purchased a ticket and bought a ticket to go and watch a match from outside of the region.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry notes 1,000 food and beverage businesses participated out of roughly 20,000 in the city, about 5%. Mamana says NYC Tourism did comprehensive outreach through BIDs, chambers, and restaurant associations, but participation was voluntary.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry questions low share of food businesses in World Cup promotion

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: We talked about the food and beverage businesses, a thousand local food and beverage businesses.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: What was it?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: 133,000 of the drink specials and commemorative cups were distributed to 1,000 local food and beverage businesses.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: How many food and local beverage businesses do we have in New York City?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: I don't know that I have the latest count, but it's typically around 20,000, something like that.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So roughly, I don't have a calculator in front of me, how much, with 20,000 businesses, 1,000 of those, what percentage?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: We did a very comprehensive outreach plan through bids, council, chambers, Latino Restaurant Association, the New York Hospitality Alliance, Hospitality Association, our member base.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: We went to non-members.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: We went all throughout the city looking for participation as best we could.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: It is voluntary, but we tried to really put a full court press on outreach.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Found a calculator.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry points to a 6% increase in Queens visitor spending despite a large fan fest and says the Bronx and Staten Island were not mentioned. Honda says the city was proud to make the Queens fan fest free and accessible, and Mamana notes the data came from Visa card spending.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry challenges weak outer-borough visitor spending gains

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: There were fan fests in all five boroughs, and I'm thankful that there was some activity outside of Manhattan, with one of the largest fan fests being in my district in Queens, in a stadium that holds over 25,000 people.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Do you think 6% economic activity during that time is a win?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Let alone, I don't even think the Bronx and Staten Island, I don't even think you guys had a trickle, a blip.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Sorry, the 6% you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Do you mind elaborating on that?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: It says, broader evidence, visitor activity extended beyond Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: International visitor spending increased 19% in Brooklyn and 6% in Queens.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Bronx and Staten Island aren't mentioned, but 6% in Queens, where we hosted a fan fest for, I want to say, almost like three weeks in a stadium that hosts over 25,000 people.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: Appreciate that question.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: I'll say we were really proud to work with the FIFA host committee to make sure that that fan fest was free and thus maximally accessible to both the surrounding community and visitors from out of town to drive maximum folks into the borough and to be

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: celebrating the World Cup accordingly.

chapters.summary: Mamana says the visitor spending figures were pulled from Visa card data. Thomas-Henry asks whether the city will pull other sources, and Mamana says it can but there are additional costs and American Express data was not used.
chapters.title: Mamana says borough spending data came only from Visa

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: The numbers that we cited for spend, for visitor spend, was pulled from Visa card data.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: So we will only include Visa card.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: That's the source we were able to pull.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Are we looking at pulling data from any other sources to see what the true impact was?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: We can do that.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: There are additional costs to doing that.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: American Express also offers that, but we were able to get it most quickly from Visa.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I'll move on.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks whether it was fair to expedite infrastructure projects without community board or community input. Honda says the city was excited about long-term improvements but needs to get back on process specifics.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry questions expedited infrastructure without community input

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Czar, you had mentioned some of the great infrastructure projects related to the World Cup that was done.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And while I know many of my colleagues in many communities may have appreciated it,

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: but do you think it was fair or appropriate to expedite city-related infrastructure projects without any community board or community input or heads up that it was happening?

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: We were very, very excited to be able to create long-term improvements to city infrastructure across the five boroughs for the support of visitor travel as well as resident travel.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And that was extremely important to us was to see that long-term benefit.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: As far as the process, I would need to get back to you on the specifics of the process, but our hope is that it continues to be of benefit to both folks in the surrounding communities who can hopefully benefit from safer bus lanes or faster buses,

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: or safer bike lanes, sorry, and faster buses, as well as future visitors.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay, and the genesis of that question is one of those bike lanes was in the adjacent community, but sits in the community board that I represent, which is Community Board 3, where there was a bus lane put in to expedite travel from LaGuardia Airport.
