utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: While I see the sense of getting visitors, it was a hardship to community, and there was no insight or input or just a heads up.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: We understand that getting travelers around safely and more efficiently works, but also

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: in that same corridor, there was nothing done to improve access to the number seven line, where visitors going to the FanFest in Queens could have stopped at, say, 103rd Street and visited.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Corona Plaza.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Currently that station, you can't even get off there if you're coming in from Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So just to look at things.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: that would infrastructure that would help the communities and not just the visitors coming to New York City.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry says infrastructure was expedited but businesses had difficulty getting permits. Honda says the city balanced safety and events and provided resources for small businesses, then turns to SBS for more detail.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry asks why infrastructure moved faster than small business permits

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And a question kind of to piggyback off that, it was easy to expedite infrastructure plans, but harder for businesses to get permits.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: To help benefit them during the World Cup.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Any insight into why we were able to move more effectively and efficiency for infrastructure for visitors, but weren't able to give our small businesses the same access to opportunities to

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: help their businesses during this time?

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: I want to speak, I'll speak a little bit to the permit question and would also love to turn it over to Harris to talk about the ways in which we engaged with small businesses to make sure they could benefit from the World Cup.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: We'll just note that, you know, PD officers worked hard throughout the entire tournament to keep New Yorkers and visitors alike safe.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And we owe them all a debt of gratitude for their tireless efforts.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And we worked both with PD, but also a host of agencies to determine which events were feasible amidst a suite of summer programming.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And so happy to find more information about specifics, but we were balancing

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: the range of keeping people safe, allowing joyous events to occur, and provided lots of resources for folks, especially small businesses, to host their own events.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And I will let Hara speak to that.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And then also I think Nancy can probably say more about the toolkit as well.

chapters.summary: Dynishal Gross thanks Honda and says SBS was in close coordination on SAPO permitting decisions. She says SBS briefed business improvement districts and merchants associations as decisions were made.
chapters.title: SBS official Dynishal Gross describes coordination with BIDs on permits

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Councilmember, for your question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: I do want to take a moment to acknowledge all that our World Cup czar just mentioned on the complexity of the summer, a summer that we will never forget thanks to her work and the efforts of city workers across this government.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: And I also wanted to acknowledge and thanking her for her work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: Whenever decisions were being made around SAPO permitting processes, there was more clarity coming out as a result of all of the complex coordination work that was necessary to keep New Yorkers safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: The minute these things were happening, we were in close coordination.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: SBS would be notified.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: We would work together in briefing the business improvement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: districts across the city as well as other merchants associations that are involved with street activations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: Obviously not everyone was able to do all the events that they wanted to do because of a summer of a lifetime that we were experiencing, but wanted to really acknowledge that there was a conscious effort made at every step of the way that as decisions were made,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: there was no gap between the time that business improvement districts and merchants associations were then hearing of the decisions that were reached as a result of the capacity needs during the summer.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry says the administration was new and had only six months before the World Cup, then asks whether it was as successful as it could have been. Honda says the World Cup was an enormous success but acknowledges the administration wishes it had started earlier.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry asks if World Cup was as successful as possible

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And I do appreciate the outreach.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I know you had come before this committee several times in preparing for World Cup, and it was literally a new administration, and it was six months later is the World Cup.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So I understand there was a lot of planning and do appreciate the outreach.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So my next question, it's not a right or wrong, and don't take it any bad way.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: But do you think it was as successful as it could have been?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I mean, as we've heard, our businesses didn't have the opportunities that they would have liked, and not just our small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: We had organizations that hosted block parties annually, and because we were getting ready for this large event and visitors, they were no longer to do what they had done in their hometown year after year after year.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And in addition to do if you think it was successful, what can we do differently, i.e.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: 2028 when the Olympics come?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: How what are the lessons learned from the World Cup that we're going to take to 2028?

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: Deeply appreciate that question.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And it's the question we should.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: all be asking ourselves and looking forward to working together on future major events.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: I think we believe that the World Cup was an enormous success.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: It was a boom for the city's economy, adding $2 billion to the local economy, supporting over 12,000 jobs, and increasing foot traffic to our sports bars by 16%.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: It was also a celebration for everyone, right?

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: We had more than 100 free watch parties across the cities with our parks, plazas, and public markets hosting tens of thousands of people.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And really want to shout out EDC activating public markets.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: Really want to shout out New York City Tourism and SBS.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: We had a borough grant program for borough presidents to support local businesses in their area and host events.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And we turned city streets into pickup games, opened up our soccer fields throughout the entire night so that people could play 24-7, thus increasing access to recreational space for folks who don't ordinarily get that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And we really tried to focus on the five boroughs, right?

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: So we drove foot traffic across all five boroughs and saw the stats that you mentioned and I think would really note when it comes to lessons learned.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: We've talked a lot about this and also welcome others'perspective here.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: We came in in January, and as you mentioned, the World Cup started in June.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And so I do think that there was a lot that was constrained by or guided by decisions of a previous administration, which is exactly what it is.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And with that in mind, we strove to work 24-7 to make sure that this was a joyful celebration for the city and the city benefited.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: So I don't think it will surprise anyone to hear it.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: that a reflection is we wish we had been mayor one year ago and would be able to start earlier.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And I think that's absolutely what we plan to do for future events, the Olympics, hopefully the Women's World Cup many years in the future.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And just thinking through how we can make sure that major events with the proper advanced planning can really benefit our small businesses as well as the residents of New York.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: I would also add that a lesson learned that we spoke about on the coordination side was the benefit of having coordination directly in City Hall to make sure that across agencies, both for logistics, preparedness, infrastructure, but also for a coordinated campaign.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: That stretched out the city and enabled the city to celebrate and was that point of contact for the host committee, for New Jersey, New York, in the region, I think was of enormous benefit to the city and really led to things being able to move very quickly in the time that we had.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And happy to also turn it over to anyone else for other reflections and would also love to hear from y'all's perspective.

chapters.summary: Mamana says NYC Tourism would have started earlier on international visitation if funding had come sooner. She says the campaign still produced positive borough dispersion and intent to visit Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx, and Staten Island.
chapters.title: Mamana reflects on tourism planning timeline and international visitors

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: I would love to pile on to that point.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: We put together our initial proposal for our incremental funding about a year prior.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Had we started then, and this is all hindsight, but it's good learning for the future, we would have started really focusing on driving international visitation at that time because the planning windows are longer for international visitors.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: They spend more, they're valuable, and that's very strategic.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: We know when folks from Canada versus Japan

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: typically tend to plan.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: By the time

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: this really kicked in, which was really at the end of March, we had to shift.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: And that's okay.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: I think we got different KPIs out of this.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: We were not able, the occupancy and demand were fairly flat, but we did see increases in the boroughs, not in Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: So that's great.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: However, I think the dispersion was what we really focused on with every opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: And we did see positive impact across every tactic.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: When we partnered with NBC and Telemundo, we did not focus on Broadway and Times Square.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: We focused on Mott Haven.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: We saw almost a 44% increase in intent to visit Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: We saw a 40% increase intent to go to Queens, 24% in the Bronx, 13% in Staten Island.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: This is impactful because it primes the pump for us moving forward.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: So now we get ready to do a campaign in the fall that goes into next year.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: We're going to leverage the digital media and the audiences that we built and the momentum we built.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: So it was a very positive experience.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: I think a lot of folks saw the organic content that came up in social media.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: People had a wonderful time here.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: So we're leveraging it.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: I think we feel it was successful from a dispersion perspective.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: But I think we would have shifted a little bit if we had more time on really driving that visitor when we were experiencing a lot of headwinds with international travel going in.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: So all in, I think that and the coordinated campaign really helped amplify the message when we're all saying the same thing at the same time.

chapters.summary: Kreamer says EDC organized 28 events, using 25 public markets that are almost entirely New York City-based small businesses. He also says EDC used the World Cup to pitch visiting businesses on opening offices in New York.
chapters.title: Kreamer highlights EDC public market events and business attraction

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Yeah, you want to add?

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Yeah, just a couple of quick things to add.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: I would say this administration made it clear from the very beginning that we wanted to bring the World Cup to New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And so a big lesson from EDC, but our colleagues as well, was how do we use city assets to accomplish that goal?

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And so with an EDC, we organized 28 events, and we used 25 of them in our public markets because our public markets are great places that are

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: community centers and are largely made up of businesses, almost 100% of businesses based in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So that's one, leveraging city assets to bring the benefits of the World Cup to all five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And then the other one is, and the czar mentioned this in her opening testimony, is much like UNGA, which was here last week and other large-scale events happened in New York,

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: It's not just tourists who come to New York City during events like this.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: It's also businesses and business owners and investors.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: It's a chance for us to really showcase New York as a place to invest in and to open a business in.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And so we took the opportunity, stepping away from the fun of the games, to bring together the business community that was visiting New York City to really sell them and pitch them on New York City

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: in hopes that part of the long tail of the World Cup would be these businesses would open up offices in New York, employ New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Contribute tax revenue, et cetera.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry tells the administration to consult small business partners, BIDs, and chambers and start planning now for 2028. She says tourism should promote neighborhoods like Mott Haven and Corona year-round, not just during the World Cup.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry urges early planning and neighborhood promotion

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Before I turn it over to my colleague, you asked for recommendations from the

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Small business side, consult our small business partners, our bids, our chambers, and the like.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Start planning now.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: 2028 to be here before we know it.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And for tourism, I think the World Cup showed us that, well, no, we know New York is a dynamic city in all five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I'd argue that a lot of visitors and the, from Mott Haven to Corona, all the activity in those corridors are something for people to experience anytime, not just when they're coming in town for the World Cup.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: When Ecuador beat Germany, Junction Boulevard in my district was one of the hottest places to be.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So when you're promoting New York City to travelers, promote our neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: They're there.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: They're bustling.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: They're thriving.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And we need that economic activity to sustain our small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And with that, I'll turn it over to Councilmember Banks for questions.

chapters.summary: Chris Banks notes the city invested $90 million and brought back $2 billion, then focuses on public housing residents. He asks whether NYCHA residents were included in employment, procurement, vending, or business outreach strategies.
chapters.title: Council Member Banks questions World Cup benefits for NYCHA residents

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you, Chiz, for this important committee.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: $90 million invested by the city, $2 billion brought back to the New York City economy.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Good job, guys.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Let me, first of all, relegate it to public housing.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And I think this is important when we have close to 511,000, a little under

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: 500,000 residential, a little over 500,000 residential living public housing, 87,000 in Brooklyn, close to 86,000 in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: 30,000 in Queens, 9,000 in Staten Island, 86,000 in Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Recently, there was a survey done by the CSS, Community Service Society, which showed that the unemployment rate in public housing is anywhere between 20% to 22%.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And we know that the unemployment rate amongst NITRA residents is higher than the overall rate citywide.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Specifically, when it comes to public housing, I want to understand whether NITRA residents were specifically included in the city's World Cup employment, procurement, or vending, or business outreach strategies.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And was there any direct partnership with EDC and New York City Housing Authority?

chapters.summary: Kreamer begins explaining the $20 million and $15 million allocations but Banks asks him to be specific to NYCHA. Kreamer says he does not have the information and suggests the host committee may be able to answer.
chapters.title: Banks presses for NYCHA employment and contracting data

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: I'll start off by just providing context on the spending itself.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So the previous administration provided $20 million for the World Cup, and then the current administration provided an additional $15 million.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Of that amount of money, the...

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: That money was then allocated for the use of the host committee.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: The host committee contract with EDC through the city was based off a 2018.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I need you to be specific to NYCHA.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Were there any NYCHA residents who obtained employment or contracting opportunities connected?

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: That was a long wind up.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So I would say that the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: If you can bring the data, if you have to go find the data and bring it back, we'll appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I'd rather you, if you don't have it now.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: I do not have the information, but I was just going to say that after us, the head of the host committee will be here and he may be able to answer that question as well.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Well, I'll just get this for the record as well.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: You know, were there any NITRO resident-owned businesses who participated, who were part of the city or the host committee initiatives?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Any?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: NITR residents who own businesses.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: I can look into that data and get it for you.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: I'll note that we worked with tourism and conventions to provide $75,000 grants to each borough president to facilitate watch parties and events across each borough.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And that included a variety of partnerships.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And so that's probably where we'll be digging in.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So it will specifically show any connection or affiliation with NITR residents.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: Yeah, we can get back to you.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Banks asks whether any World Cup youth, workforce, or small business programming took place directly in NYCHA developments. Honda says the city can get that information and notes $75,000 grants to borough presidents for watch parties.
chapters.title: Banks asks about World Cup programming in NYCHA developments

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Did any World Cup-related programming, youth initiative, or workforce event, or small business campaign take place directly within any of the NITRA developments?

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: We can get you that information.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Go ahead.

chapters.summary: Dynishal Gross says SBS prioritized outreach in Black, brown, and immigrant communities, including public housing areas in Staten Island, Queens, and Brooklyn. She says SBS canvassed over 1,800 businesses, including street vendors.
chapters.title: SBS describes outreach to public housing and immigrant communities

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember, for your question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: So at SBS, we were the outreach arm for the city's efforts to promote and ensure that small businesses were getting connected to all of the promotional opportunities that were being unlocked through either the host committee.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So did you do any outreach to Michigan?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: We did outreach.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: We prioritized outreach in black and brown communities and immigrant communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: We were in Jackson Heights, in Port Richmond, in Harlem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: We went to Jamaica, Almers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: We went to so many different communities in the outer boroughs, in neighborhoods where we know, especially for the immigrant-owned.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: community concentrations, the threats from the non-local law enforcement had created a...

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: But I'm specifically talking about public housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: Yes, so including...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: So I just want you to...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: ...Public housing in North Shore, Staten Island, in Queens, in Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: We visited, and collectively across all of those efforts, we reached over 1,800 businesses that we canvassed, including street vendors.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Banks asks whether NYCHA community centers, resident associations, or youth programs received funding for watch parties or soccer clinics. Honda says she can get exact numbers and notes the city resourced HHS shelters for watch parties.
chapters.title: Banks asks about funding for NYCHA watch parties and youth programs

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Were NYCHA community centers or resident associations or youth programs offered funding or other resources to organize local watch parties, soccer clinics, or related programming?

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: I can get you exact numbers on that.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: I will note that we resourced HHS to host watch parties at the city's remaining asylum seeker shelters and eight shelters for families with children.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay, excellent.

chapters.summary: Banks asks for total World Cup contracts and subcontracts awarded to New York City businesses, MWBEs, businesses outside Manhattan, small businesses, street vendors, and NYCHA resident-owned businesses. He also asks about payment delays and disputes.
chapters.title: Banks requests contract, MWBE, and payment data for World Cup vendors

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And what was the total value of the war cup related contracts and subcontracts awarded to city businesses?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Chairs, if you may indulge me for a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: You go on ahead.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: What were those contracts?

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So the total amount that was allocated to the...

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: The total value of the World Cup contracts and subcontracts awarded to New York City businesses.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So we'll have to get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And I guess of the total, how much were awarded to the MWBEs?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: How much was awarded to businesses located outside of Manhattan?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: How much was awarded to businesses with fewer than 50 employees?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: How much was awarded to street vendors and NITRA residents'own businesses, which we brought that up earlier?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: How long did small vendors and subcontracts have to wait for payment for World Cup-related work?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Are any invoices or payments still outstanding?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Were any payment disputes filed?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And have any businesses reported that they...

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: have not yet been fully compensated.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: We can get you the exact details on that.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: I will note that the $75,000 borough president grants also supported the Queens Night Market and a watch party on Governor's Island with a street vendor fair and other such events.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And so we can get you the information around that.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: We'll be waiting for your information.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Numbers for Nitra.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And then in my last...

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry interrupts to move questioning to Council Member Marano. Banks says he will come back later.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry moves to Council Member Marano

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Councilmember Banks, we have a...

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I'll come back in a second.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: There you go.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Round two.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Councilmember Marano.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Frank Morano says he is often critical of the administration but credits it for capturing $2 billion despite no matches in New York City. He asks how much of that $2 billion actually went to independently owned New York City small businesses.
chapters.title: Council Member Morano credits administration but asks where money went

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I wasn't going to rush you.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I thought you were great.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you all for your testimony and for your work.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You know, I am the first person to be critical of the administration when warranted.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So I do think it's important for me to say, and for all of us, that the administration deserves a great deal of credit here.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: The New York City didn't host a single World Cup match, yet according to the preliminary analysis released today, the city captured $2 billion in economic impact.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: That's pretty significant.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So congratulations to all of you for that.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But while we have all of you here, all the people that made that happen, I'd like to get beyond the big number and kind of follow up with what some of my colleagues were touching upon, and that's where the money actually went.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So that headline is $2 billion in economic impact, and I appreciate, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Kramer, the differentiation.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: between indirect activity and other types of economic activity.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If I'm a restaurant owner on Highland Boulevard, I can't necessarily deposit economic impact at the bank.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Of that $2 billion,

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: How much can we say actually went to independently owned New York City small businesses, not hotels generally, not induced economic activity, not national chains?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Do we know how many dollars actually went through the cash registers of New York City small businesses?

chapters.summary: Kreamer says the $2 billion analysis does not break down spending to independently owned small businesses. Morano asks whether the city should decide beforehand to measure how much economic benefit reaches small businesses for future mega events.
chapters.title: Morano presses for small business revenue metrics for future events

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: The $2 billion analysis that you're referring to doesn't break the information down to that level.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Anybody else?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: Councilmember, so defer to our colleagues at the Economic Development Corporation on the economic analysis they conducted, but it was too easy when you mentioned Highland Boulevard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: There's a burger joint that just opened up, CD Burger, and the first, as they were doing their grand opening, they were featuring a World Cup game.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: And so part of the reason folks came to that grand opening was not just the delicious burgers they were serving, but because they had a FIFA World Cup game on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: And that's the type of engagement we saw throughout the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: It was really a summer where, whether it was at the businesses, where you saw record levels of engagement and attendance, and business owners anecdotally

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: have shared their experiences with the summer, where it was the Knicks championship run, then game after game, but it was also in the homes of many of our family members where we're ordering from businesses.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: No, and I've had similar anecdotal observations, but if nobody, if none of the agencies can...

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Necessarily answer that question of how much went to New York City small businesses, shouldn't that be one of the lessons of this World Cup?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: For the next mega event, whether it's the Olympics or something else, shouldn't we decide beforehand

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: that we're going to measure how much of that economic benefit

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: if it actually reaches small businesses, and then come up with a metric or a series of metrics to determine how we're going to get there.

chapters.summary: Kreamer says the $2 billion analysis is initial and Tourism Economics will provide a sector breakdown. He says EDC will also conduct a small business survey with SBS, BIDs, and NYC Tourism to measure revenue lifts and hiring.
chapters.title: Kreamer promises sector breakdown and small business survey

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Yeah, a couple of points to your comments, and thank you for them.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: One is the analysis that was released this morning, the $2 billion one, is an initial analysis.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: There will be additional information that Tourism Economics will be sharing with us, including a breakdown by sector.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Again, it does not go down to the level that you're looking for, but we'll know lodging, retail, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So we'll have that information.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: We'll be happy to share with you all once that is available.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Second point is, as part of our contract with Tourism Economics, we are going to be conducting a survey of small businesses around the city as well.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: We'll be partnering with SBS, the bids, and other groups, NYC Tourism, of course, to do that post-mortem, as you just mentioned, to find out how many people...

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: From the participation, how many people saw a lift in revenue, did they hire additional people, those type of questions.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So we would be pleased to work with you all to make sure that the survey gets out, because that information and data that comes back in will be really helpful for us to then help plan for 2028 for the Olympics and hopefully 2031 for the Women's World Cup.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: We're also surveying the thousand or so businesses that participated in the Five Borough of the Cup program, winter special.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: We only have 68 so far, but we're working on it.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: So, yeah, similarly, we'd love to work with you.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: We want to.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Make sure there was a return, and that's how we're going to find out.

chapters.summary: Morano notes only 28 Staten Island businesses participated in the Five Borough Winner Special compared with 589 in Manhattan. He asks whether anyone in city government monitored participation and tried to increase low borough numbers.
chapters.title: Morano questions low Staten Island participation and lack of dashboard

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Chair Thomas Henry was kind enough to mention Staten Island, and I appreciate your testimony that says nearly 1,000 businesses participated in the Five Borough Winners Special.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But the breakdown was 589 Manhattan, 182 Brooklyn, 152 Queens, 33 in the Bronx, and 28 in Staten Island.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So my question is not, why did you discriminate against Staten Island?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I certainly don't think anybody did.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: My question is a little more basic.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Did anybody notice?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So while this program was happening, was anybody in city government looking at a dashboard that said, we've got 589 businesses in Manhattan, 28 on Staten Island,

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: maybe we ought to make some calls or do something to up that 28 number to 30, 35, 40?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And who specifically owned that responsibility?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Is it you, Madam Zahr?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Is it tourism?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Is it SBS?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Is it somebody else?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Because I think there's a larger lesson here.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I think if there's something we can measure after a government ends, after a government observation ends,

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: It should be something we manage while the program is happening.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I think that's also a lesson for the next event as well.

chapters.summary: Mamana says she agrees with Morano and that outreach was largely manual through associations, BIDs, and chambers. She says with more time the city could have started earlier and kept a better tally.
chapters.title: Mamana acknowledges manual outreach and need for earlier start

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: I think I completely agree.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: I don't know that we had a live dashboard, but I have three pages of businesses that we've reached out to in terms of associations, bids.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: It's largely a manual process, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: So we try to multiply it by going through the bids and chambers and the restaurant associations.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: I think with the time we had, again, not to punt that question, but I think if we had an

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: additional timing, we probably could have started earlier and began to do a little bit more on the outreach and try to kind of keep that tally going so we were properly balanced when we launched the program.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry says her office offered to help distribute cups and wants small businesses to succeed. She then turns questioning over to Council Member Brooks-Powers.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry offers council help and moves to Brooks-Powers

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thanks very much.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And I'll say, I don't want to speak for my other colleagues, but I know my office called and was like, just bring us the cups.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: We'll drop them off.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So you have resources.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: We want to help because we want to see our small businesses succeed.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: At this time, I'll turn it over to Councilmember Brooks Powers.

chapters.summary: Selvena Brooks-Powers asks whether the city formally requested the $1 million FIFA legacy contribution and whether it would invest it in soccer pitches or youth programs. She also asks about lodging data and Queens business participation.
chapters.title: Council Member Brooks-Powers questions FIFA legacy funds and Queens outreach

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you, chairs, and thank you for your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: My first question centers around return on the city's investment.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Has the city formally requested the $1 million legacy contribution from FIFA?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: If it is paid, will the city commit to investing it in soccer pitches or youth programs?

chapters.summary: Honda says she is not sure if the city formally requested the $1 million from FIFA but says conversations about legacy are ongoing. She says the host committee is building pitches and the city wants accessible opportunities to play.
chapters.title: Honda says city in conversations about FIFA legacy and soccer pitches

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: I can get you more information.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: I'm not sure if we've formally requested it from FIFA, that we've been in conversation about legacy.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And I know that the host committee is building many pitches and has built at least, I can let them answer that question, but

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: many pitches are in the process of being built in the five boroughs and would add that we're in ongoing conversations about what the legacy of the World Cup looks like, both from the infrastructure perspective and from the investment perspective.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And we'll note that we absolutely want to make sure that

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: a legacy invests in accessible opportunities to play for New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: Absolutely.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers says hotel revenue rose because room rates increased, not necessarily because more people stayed. She asks whether NYC Tourism tracks how many World Cup visitors stayed outside the city because they could not find or afford lodging.
chapters.title: Brooks-Powers asks whether hotel revenue came from rates or occupancy

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Next, I want to pivot to lodging and visitor spending.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Hotel revenue rose because room rates went up, not necessarily because more people stayed here.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Does New York City Tourism track

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: how many World Cup visitors stayed outside the city because they couldn't find or afford a place to stay in New York, and what did the data that you do have show?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we only track what's happening in the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers notes about 60% of Five Borough Winner Special businesses were in Manhattan and asks how many were in Queens, Southeast Queens, and the Rockaways. Mamana says there were 152 in Queens and she can provide a neighborhood breakdown.
chapters.title: Brooks-Powers requests Queens and Rockaway business participation data

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Reaching Queens businesses and neighborhoods, and this is for SBS,

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: About 60% of five borough winners'special businesses were in Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: How many participants were in Queens and how many in Southeast Queens and the Rockaways specifically?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Do you want to be?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: I can take that.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: We have 152 in Queens total.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: I do have a complete list of participants, so I can come back to you with that, where it all breaks down by neighborhoods that go within.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Will you be able to do a while we're in the hearing?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I have a number in my mind.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I just want to see if it is in alignment.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I brought the spreadsheet, but I definitely will follow up with you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers notes Citi Field will host nine Olympic soccer matches in 2028 and asks whether the city will require local hiring, MWBE, local procurement, and security cost commitments before funding. Kreamer says planning has not started but lessons will apply.
chapters.title: Brooks-Powers asks about local hiring and MWBE commitments for 2028 Olympics

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: EDC.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Etad Park in Queens will host nine Olympic soccer matches in 2028.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Before committing city funds, will the city require local hiring, MWBE, and local procurement

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: commitments and a clear share of security costs borne by the organizers?

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So this administration for this World Cup was committed to making sure that the benefits reached all five boroughs of New York City, including women-owned, minor-owned businesses, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And so while the planning for 2020 has not started, the lessons learned from this World Cup will be applied for that.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And it's something that we will definitely look into and we'll seek to achieve.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks whether MWBE participation and opportunity data from the World Cup has been made public. Kreamer says the host committee, which will testify next, has the best tabulations of where money went.
chapters.title: Kreamer says host committee holds MWBE participation data

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Have you guys made public the data from what we recently just completed in terms of like the, particularly the MBE?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Participation and opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So that information is best to be asked to the host committee who will be testifying next as they're the ones who

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: EDC served as the as the disbursement vehicle or reversement vehicle for the funding, but they would have the best.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Tabulations of where all the money went to in terms of that type of breakdown.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Understood.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks what SBS will do differently so Queens small businesses outside the stadium area have materials in their languages from day one. Gross says SBS used email, webinars, door-to-door canvassing, and reached over 280,000 New Yorkers.
chapters.title: SBS describes multilingual outreach for Queens small businesses

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And then lastly for SBS, what will SBS do differently so that Queens small businesses, especially those outside the immediate stadium area, have materials and outreach in their languages from day one?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: We were really excited to engage the minute NYC Tourism and SBS landed on the business toolkit, which included all the different promotional materials.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: We went on a multimodal outreach campaign.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: We did email marketing, webinars, door-to-door canvassing across our five boroughs, and we collectively reached over 280,000 New Yorkers to ensure that they were educated and the opportunities that were available.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: In those two months, even when we were doing corridor walks with council members, many of you have to remember

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: that one pager that we were bringing to our walks with elected officials, but that was just one vehicle of six, seven different mechanisms by which we were making sure New Yorkers were hearing and learning about the opportunities by which they could help promote their businesses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: And it was exciting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: We did not make assumptions on the types of businesses that would want to be featured on tourism's calendar, and we had a...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: Relatively new bubble tea shop in Astoria, Queens that decided a day before the start of the World Cup games that they would actually go really hard on the World Cup and do a bunch of watch parties.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: And by knowing about the calendar, they were able to quickly sign up.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks again whether the city will commit the $1 million FIFA legacy contribution to soccer pitches and youth programs if paid. Honda says she will get back but values are aligned and the city is considering lighting and programming existing fields.
chapters.title: Brooks-Powers asks city to commit FIFA legacy funds to youth soccer

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And just going back to the World Cup czar briefly, the second part of the question wasn't answered in terms of, I know you got a follow-up on the $1 million, but in the event that it is going to be paid,

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Is the city willing to commit to investing in the soccer pitches and youth programs?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I wasn't clear on that part.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: I will have to get back to you.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: I think absolutely in terms of values we are aligned.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: I will note that one thing we are thinking about when it comes to building new pitches is that right now we have a lot of pitches that don't have lighting, for example.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And so expanding access may look like more than just building a new field.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: It may look like programming for existing fields, expanding lighting hours.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: There are many ways that that money can be invested well to increase access for young people and increase program opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: I can't commit just because I'm not certain of what the details would look like, but that is absolutely our priority and our goal.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I'll just say it shouldn't be either or, it should be and.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Because, like, for example, community, I've been getting a lot of incoming from Rockaway schools wanting to see.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Soccer brought there.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: We have a new school being built that's opening soon that has a soccer field that they created, but that's for that school.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: But just wanting to have more public spaces for that and other parts of Southeast Queens as well.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairs.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry thanks Brooks-Powers and turns questioning to Council Member Riley.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry moves to Council Member Riley

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Councilmember Riley.

chapters.summary: Kevin Riley thanks the panel and says $2 billion is impressive but is disappointed the Bronx had only 28 participating businesses. He asks about local hiring and the types of occupations created during the World Cup.
chapters.title: Council Member Riley questions Bronx participation and job creation

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairs, for this meeting.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you so much for the panel.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I just want to echo the sentiments of my colleagues, especially Councilman Banks.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I think you guys did a tremendous job.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And under a limited time, $2 billion investments is amazing.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I am a little bit disappointed being from the Bronx that 28 was the number that we were given.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I think.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Opportunities for out-of-borough connection when we have large-scale events like this needs to be a little bit more fleshed out.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We have beautiful communities in the city.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: The Bronx, City Island alone took a lot of people there during this time.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So I just wanted to share that sentiment and see how we could, I guess, connect in the future when we see the Olympics coming here on how we can make that a little bit better.

chapters.summary: Riley asks whether there is a breakdown of local residents hired and the occupations they filled. Kreamer says the 12,100 jobs figure comes from a Tourism Economics model and does not go down to that level of detail.
chapters.title: Riley asks for local hiring and occupation breakdown

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I wanted to talk about job creation.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I know during the largest thing that we always or the benefit from large events like this is job creation.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Is there a breakdown on the local residents who were hired during the World Cup?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And do you have a breakdown of the type of occupations that they were hired for?

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: We don't have a breakdown of that information.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: The 12,100 jobs was based off of a model that Tourism Economics uses, but it's not.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: It doesn't go down to that level of detail.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Riley says large events can burden communities through street closures and disrupted block parties. He asks what steps the city is taking to prevent residents and small businesses from bearing disproportionate burdens.
chapters.title: Riley asks how city will prevent burdens on residents and small businesses

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Large-scale events could also be a burden on communities.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I know we did a lot of planning.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: There was a lot of street closures.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Trust me, block parties were a big thing in our districts, and they could have happened because of this event.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So what are the steps that the city is taking to prevent residents and small businesses from bearing the disproportionate burden from events like this?

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: I would also love for SBS to speak a little bit to the outreach that we did around toolkits and kind of preparing for the World Cup.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: But we'll note that we were working very closely with bids and we want to make sure, I think, with more time, could work more closely and be continuing that conversation.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And so looking forward to 2028 planning, but really wanted to work closely with folks to get out the word about how to apply for a permit when a permit is not required, all of those pieces.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And I think we did a variety of multimodal outreach, whether it was the small business toolkit, working with city council members, working with bids to get the word out.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And I'll let you speak more.

chapters.summary: Gross says SBS worked with the World Cup czar and FDNY on a social media video reaching over 50,000 New Yorkers about business preparedness. She says SBS promoted the NYC Business Express Service Team for one-on-one compliance consultations.
chapters.title: SBS describes outreach on permits and business compliance

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member, for your question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: I'd also like to add, so while there may be, by not having the ability for every single neighborhood, every single commercial quarter to have a block party, that does potentially create the risk of having,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: but also benefit an opportunity for small businesses to absorb more of that traffic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: So what we were really excited to do with our czar and the FDNY commissioner was do a social media video that reached over 50,000 New Yorkers on for small business owners to tell them, look, we're in this World Cup season.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: This brings a tremendous opportunity to you, but you should also know all of the things you should do to protect your business from the surge of visitors and ensuring that you're complying and making sure

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: fire safety is maintained, making sure you're doing everything that's possible and promoting our

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: New York City Business Express Service Team, which provides one-on-one compliance consultations to these business owners to ensure that they have everything that they need and they're prepared on day one to absorb the kind of customers that we saw throughout the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: And it's exciting, even if a neighborhood did not have a SAPO permit issued, there were neighborhoods where people went in droves after the games, during the games, and sometimes created conditions on the commercial quarter, but oftentimes were

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: packing all of the small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: And I can only think of Bay Ridge and Astoria, and we talked about Junction Boulevard, all the neighborhoods where we saw tremendous economic...

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: White Plains Road.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: And White Plains Road, yes.

chapters.summary: Riley says many visitors stayed across the Hudson in New Jersey and asks whether the city tracks short-term rentals or homeowner hosting. Mamana says NYC Tourism does not track Airbnb data.
chapters.title: Riley asks about tracking visitors staying in New Jersey and Airbnbs

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Lastly, I believe the chief marketing officer stated that you guys are only tracking what's happening here in the five boroughs when it comes to lodging.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I would encourage to see what's happening because we do know a lot of people did stay across the Hudson in New Jersey during this World Cup, even though they wanted to stay in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Did you guys also track outside of hotels, maybe short-term rentals with homeowners?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Is that also data that's being tracked that was being utilized during the World Cup?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Yeah, unfortunately, no, we don't track Airbnb data at all.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I think you should look into that possibly because I do know we got a lot.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I represent a home ownership district, and they wanted to benefit from the World Cup as well.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And that could have put.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: tremendous restraints on a lot of them from doing it because of the current model.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So if we could just look into that as well.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairs.

chapters.summary: Maloney returns to spending questions and cites $35 million through EDC, $4.5 million to NYC Tourism, and $50.2 million to NYPD. She asks for final spending figures broken out by agency.
chapters.title: Maloney asks for final agency spending breakdown of $90M

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I want to dig into a bit of the spending questions on where the city's $90 million went.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: On my end, I have $35 million that went through EDC and primarily was passed through the host committee.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: 4.5 million to NYC tourism, 50.2 million to the NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Could you share the final spending figures on how they were broken out by agency, if there are any changes from what I just shared?

chapters.summary: Kreamer confirms $35 million was allocated to the host committee, which spent about $33.4 million. He says the remaining $1.5 million was used by the city for community events and branding, and describes host committee spending categories.
chapters.title: Kreamer details host committee spending categories

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Sure, I can start off with the $35 million portion that you referenced, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So yes, you're correct, $35 million was allocated for the host committee.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: They ultimately ended up spending about $33.4, $3.5 million of it.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: That remaining balance, $1.6, $1.5, was used by the city instead for community events, branding, dressing the city type of activities.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: For the host committee itself, the scope of work that they were asked to execute upon was largely broken out into, sorry, broken out into

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: four different areas.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: The first is the actual cost for operating the nonprofit that was set up as the host committee.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Two is the fan zones themselves.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Three is promotional activities to get people to come and be aware and to get people to go to visit the five boroughs while they're here.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So promotional activities.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And then fourth is the operational logistics as it relates to safety, transportation, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So those are the four categories of spending.

chapters.summary: Honda says some agency budgets were repurposed and additional funding went to NYSEM for daily operational calls. She says the city is still assessing total World Cup cost and disaggregating NYPD overtime is difficult because it overlapped with other summer events.
chapters.title: Honda discusses agency spending and NYPD overtime attribution

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And I can add from specific agencies,

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: Between Parks, DOT, NISM, and a few other agencies, I know that some of standard budget was just repurposed, for example, around programming, can get you those numbers.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: But additional funding did go to NISM, which stood up, for example, these daily operational calls throughout the summer to make sure between Knicks Parade, Sailforth 250th, visit of President, you name it, everything went smoothly and we're very proud of the results there.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: The note on PD overtime.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: So the World Cup was obviously a massive initiative and it stretched across multiple agencies, multiple levels of government and multiple fiscal years.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: It also overlapped with the Knicks championship, Sailforth 250th parade, a historic wedding, which sadly I was not invited to, and other regular summer programming.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And so the city is basically still assessing the overall cost of the World Cup itself, and it is somewhat difficult to disaggregate.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: But with specific questions about NYPD overtime, I would encourage you to reach out directly to the agency on that.

chapters.summary: Maloney notes the reported revenue was $414 million for city and state taxes, while Council Finance estimated city tax revenue around $60 million and the comptroller estimated $55 million. She asks when the final analysis will be available.
chapters.title: Maloney compares city tax revenue estimates and asks for final analysis

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And that is something we'll be following up on.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I'm very curious what, I think it was $50 million towards NYPD, but overtime, what percentage of that is going to be due to overtime and what percent of that is attributed to the cup?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: The revenue.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: numbers, the revenue number reported was 4.14 million for both city and state taxes.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So I'm just curious, the council finance team estimated that city tax revenue is roughly 60 million, and in an estimate from the comptroller's office, it was 55 million.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So again, just trying to balance the two sides and

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: make sure we've got the full sense of the return on investment here.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And if not today, when can we expect the final analysis?

chapters.summary: Kreamer says the $414 million state and local tax revenue figure was based on Tourism Economics analysis for the region, including New York State and New Jersey. He says it is an estimated number, not actual receipts.
chapters.title: Kreamer clarifies $414M tax estimate is regional and estimated

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: I can provide a comment on the first number you mentioned, the roughly $414 million in state and local tax revenues.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So that was based off of the tourism economics.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Analysis that was done for the region.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So that includes not just New York City, but New York State, New Jersey, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And it's not disaggregated.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: It is also largely an estimated number as well.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So the inputs that I mentioned before, timesing the amount of spend by, for lodging, for example, for beds tax and sales tax is how they came up with that number.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So it's not actual receipts in, it's an estimation.

chapters.summary: Maloney asks for a more granular sense of what share goes to New York City taxes. Kreamer says that number has not been provided yet, and Honda says the city is still evaluating costs and projected revenue with a lag in data collection.
chapters.title: Maloney presses on NYC tax share and comptroller's $55M estimate

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Do we have a more granular sense of what percent of that is going to New York City taxes after a harrowing budget negotiation last year?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: We have to have to be detailed on these types of things.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So just asking.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Yes, specifically to.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: tourism economics estimate of tax revenue.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: That number has not been provided yet, but we will be getting it.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: But I do want to emphasize that it is an estimated number.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: It is not an actual number based off of city receipts.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And do you have any comment on the comptroller's analysis?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Which placed this at $55 million and would mean that there was a loss of about $30 million in spend to revenue generated.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: So I'll note that this event stretched across multiple agencies, multiple levels of government, and multiple fiscal years.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: So we're still evaluating both the total cost of the event as well as the projected revenue.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: Estimating revenues is complex, and there is a lag in data collection.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And so we do not have enough info to estimate the World Cup's impact in sales tax collection in that level of detail at this moment.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: However, we are assessing the costs and can definitely continue to be in conversation about that as we complete the analysis.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And do we have a sense of when that would be at the end of the fiscal year?

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: I will get back to you on timeline on that.

chapters.summary: Maloney asks EDC to describe long-tail business discussions from the World Cup. Kreamer says EDC's Choose NYC program hosted a summit with 350 attendees, including 150 businesses from 34 countries considering expansion to New York.
chapters.title: Kreamer describes Choose NYC long-tail business attraction

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: One question for EDC.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: You mentioned that there's a long-tail impact of discussions that kicked off during the Cup with businesses.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: If you can speak to a few of those examples and what you expect to come of them.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you for the question, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: I would say more broadly, when thinking about the World Cup, in many ways it was an investment for the city for long-term returns, and that can come in many different ways.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: More tourists down the road, more large-scale events like this down the road, and yes, to your question, more businesses.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So we at EDC have a program called Choose NYC, and that works with...

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: It works to accomplish three things.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
