utterances.text: One is to brand New York City as open for business and to gain a pipeline of businesses who are considering coming to New York City or expanding within New York City.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And then once we have a qualified lead, we then work with that business to help connect them to resources and answer questions.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: To get them to say yes to New York City and open an office here, hire New Yorkers, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: We typically host the Choose NYC Summit, which is our flagship event at a different time of the year.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: We purposely had it during the World Cup because we knew there was going to be a lot of businesses in town.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: There were 350 attendees to the Choose NYC Summit.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: 150 of them, roughly, were businesses who are considering expanding within New York City or to New York City from 34 countries around the world.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And so we keep track of all those conversations as part of a broader effort of Choose NYC, and those conversations continue.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: To provide some context, kind of the decision timeline for a business considering coming to New York and really there.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: There are some that may take two years to decide and could be shorter than that.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: But this was really kind of a beachhead moment for us to get more businesses aware of the opportunities in New York City, what resources are there, and in hopes down the road they will open an office here.

chapters.summary: Maloney asks how NYC Tourism will capitalize on World Cup momentum amid concerns about international travel. Mamana says the programmatic media buy created a data pool for retargeting and a new campaign will launch in November.
chapters.title: Mamana explains tourism retargeting and November campaign

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: After the summer of the Knicks, I feel like that's a good sales pitch to end the cup to get those businesses to move.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Similarly for NYC tourism, how do we, as a city, plan to capitalize on the momentum from the cup where we had a lot of international travelers, particularly in the context of tourism?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Broad concerns about international travel, particularly from Canada.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So how are we going to keep moving the ball forward for NYC tourism?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: The first piece is the million dollars that we spent on the programmatic media that I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: The byproduct of that is a pool of data that we can then retarget.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: So the folks that saw our media, we can then retarget for the future.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: So for the next one to two years, we're going to continue targeting those folks and focusing our ads on them because they already showed interest in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: So whether they came or they

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: It just showed interest in the creative.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: That's a longer tail for that investment that we will leverage for the next one to two years.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: I would also say the organic content that happened on social media from visitors, we did not.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Plant them.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: We did not pay for it, but I'm sure you all saw, not just in New York, but for all the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Host cities, an incredibly positive wave of emotion toward the surprising experiences they had here and how friendly people were and how great the food was, etc.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: So we will have a new campaign launching in November that leverages that positivity and energy.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: We want to tap into a very unique moment that has happened here, and maybe we did not expect it going into the World Cup.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: We were really facing declines in international visitation across the board.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: So while we may have been fairly flat,

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: We did see great intent to visit from the media and the content we produced toward the boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: So we're taking that and we're going to keep moving forward with that because we saw results from the NBC and Telemundo content that we did and all of our social content.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Again, we really focus on the cultural communities associated with the teams playing here.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: And that's where we saw our wins.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: There are certain geopolitical issues that we're not going to solve by marketing.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: But because of the encouraging dispersion we saw and the awareness of our local neighborhoods, I mentioned St.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: George, Astoria, Mott Haven.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: This is what we focused on in our NBC and Telemundo content.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: We know there's interest, so we're going to just continue the effort.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: And I think all of that got us to, and the next certainly started us off.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: The parade was June 18th, so it really did not overlap completely.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: So I think we can really attribute the energy of the World Cup and the fandom that took us away from the sort of political dialogue that was going on previously.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: So we know that travelers enjoyed their stay, and we're going to be continuing to leverage that in the next campaign.

chapters.summary: Maloney asks whether NYC Tourism has resources to implement the strategy. Mamana says it does not have the same level of budget moving forward and relies on travel partners like airlines and tour operators to compound investment.
chapters.title: Mamana says NYC Tourism lacks resources for another big campaign

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And does NYC Tourism have the resources to implement that strategy that you just outlined?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Not as much as we would like.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: This was a much bigger effort than we typically would undertake.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: I think it's very scalable, so we don't have the same level of budgets moving forward.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: We are very resourceful, and we look to travel partners to help us compound the investment, like airlines and tour operators.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: So the more we have, the more impactful we know we can be based on the results that we just saw.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Kreamer adds that Choose NYC intentionally spread opportunity across the five boroughs. He says the summit had tabling for each borough led by chambers, a panel with chamber presidents, and site visits to the Bronx, Long Island City, and downtown Brooklyn.
chapters.title: Kreamer details Choose NYC borough chamber outreach

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Councilmember, can I add one thing to my answer before that I neglected to mention?

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: For the Choose NYC Summit and the work that we do and that work in general, we are very intentional at thinking about how do we take global economic interest in New York City and making sure that that opportunity gets spread across the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And so some of the ways that we enacted that for the Choose NYC program during the World Cup is twofold.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: At the summit itself, we had...

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Tabling for each of the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: to have materials that were led by each of the five chambers, and it also included some participation from some of the business improvement districts.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: We also had a panel discussion where the five presidents of the chambers were also speaking to the audience about the various resources and virtues of why a business should open up in their neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: We took it a step further, where the day after the conference, we organized for interested businesses a tour of different neighborhoods in New York City, and so we took businesses and what we call lead generators, so these are

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Organizations that work with businesses are making site decisions, and we brought them to the Bronx in partnership with the Bronx Chamber of Commerce.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: We brought them to Long Island City with the Long Island City Partnership.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: We brought them to downtown Brooklyn with the downtown Brooklyn Partnership.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And so those were some real ways that we are also trying to take that economic activity and bring it across the five rows during the World Cup.

chapters.summary: Maloney asks how New Yorkers responded and participated in World Cup events. Kreamer says EDC organized 28 events and nearly 7,000 New Yorkers attended public market events, while Honda cites LinkNYC match streaming, soccer streets, and 24-7 fields.
chapters.title: Panel describes New Yorkers' participation in World Cup events

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: A lot of the conversation and the analysis has focused on bringing visitors to New York and the economic impact of bringing people to the city.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: How did New Yorkers respond?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Do we have a sense of that and their participation in these events?

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: I can go first.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: So from an EDC perspective, we were very intentional in using our real estate assets to bring the joy of the World Cup to communities across the city.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And so, as I mentioned before, we organized 26 events, or sorry, 28 events across the city.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: As an example, we worked with our public markets.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Our public markets are nearly 100% small businesses that are based in New York City of that group.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Roughly 77% are minority-owned businesses and around 46% are women-owned businesses.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And so we directly...

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: Contracted with a number of them to provide programming during the events, but also to have some knock-on effects where more visitors would be going to the spaces and shop there.

utterances.speaker: Justin Kreamer
utterances.text: And in total, across our portfolio, we saw close to 7,000 New Yorkers attend those events in Brooklyn and Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: I also want to add that a lot of the initiatives that we did were also designed to target New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And I think certainly anecdotally, also in kind of social listening, you could kind of tell that a lot of New Yorkers were exploring the city, some for the first time and some just newly.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: So that was super exciting.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And I think in particular, streaming matches on Link NYC kiosks throughout the city, that was designed not for like tourists who are here to visit, but for folks who are just around the city.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And so we actually had amazing scenes of New Yorkers gathering in front of these link kiosks to watch games.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: We transformed over 50 blocks across the city into these soccer streets for New York City public schools.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: So that was a huge benefit to public school students.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And then.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: Our 24-7 soccer fields, I think, was a really exciting success where, you know, we did this pilot and we were unsure whether people would want to play soccer at four in the morning.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And it turns out that, you know, hundreds of people want to play soccer at four in the morning.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And so I think it was a really exciting pilot for, and, you know, and that's something that was majority taken advantage of by residents.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And so, again, an example of an initiative where we sort of were using the World Cup to expand access to the beautiful game, both watching and playing.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: And anecdotally, I'll just add that we know that half of our following, both for our website and our social channel, are locals.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: And I think some of that was through the pandemic and creating resources for that.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: And then the programs that we do, like Restaurant Week and Broadway Week.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: So we know we reach locals as well.

chapters.summary: Maloney says match-day truck deliveries were prohibited from 30th to 60th Streets and lanes were reserved for buses and official vehicles. She asks about economic impact and how businesses were consulted before the changes.
chapters.title: Maloney asks about Midtown truck delivery restrictions on match days

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Great, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And the ferry, the raft ferries too, was a fan favorite.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: One issue I did want to bring up as it impacted my district in Midtown East is on match days, truck deliveries were prohibited from

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: 30th to 60th streets for extended periods of time while the lanes on 5th and 6th Avenue were reserved for buses, shuttles, official vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Do you have a sense of what the economic impact was from those restrictions and also how were the businesses consulted before these changes were made and how far in advance?

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: We can get back to you on economic impact and as well as the community engagement process, though community outreach was done and we ran both campaigns for

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: kind of commuters and visitors and residents as well as doing direct outreach to businesses.

chapters.summary: Maloney says permitting was a major point of contention for community groups and BIDs trying to do local activations. Honda says more time was key, the city communicated constantly with BIDs and small businesses, and coordination could always improve.
chapters.title: Maloney asks for permitting lessons for future large events

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: That was one pain point that I heard.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: The second, I think we'll hear more about, but was on permitting.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: We talked about this in February, but the permitting process was a major point of contention as it was a big challenge for some of the community groups or the bids and brands that were trying to do local activations.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So learning from this experience, of course, more time, but what are some of the other takeaways for future large-scale events like this?

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: Thank you for your question.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: As you said, I think more time was kind of a key one here.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And so I feel really grateful to all the agencies that stepped up to do that kind of communication outward.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And we were in pretty constant communication with bids and with small businesses that were interested in hosting events.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: I think also, you know, everything is a function in the end of resources around, you know, security and being able to spend.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And so we feel really good about folks doing both informal and formal events throughout the city.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And, you know, coordination could always be improved, but definitely a lot of learnings from the process.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Maloney acknowledges Council Members Farias, Gutierrez, and Aviles. She then turns questioning back to co-chair Thomas-Henry.
chapters.title: Maloney acknowledges additional members and returns to Thomas-Henry

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I want to acknowledge we were joined by Councilmember Farias, Councilmember Gutierrez, and Councilmember Aviles, and we'll now turn to my co-chair for some more questions.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks whether the city obtained the 2025 tourism economic numbers. Mamana says they will need to come back with that information.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry asks again for 2025 tourism comparison

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Well, before we start, were we able to get those economic numbers for 2025?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: For tourism?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: No, we'll need to come back to you with that.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry notes the World Cup, Knicks parade, 250th anniversary, and Jay-Z concert all happened in July. She asks whether the city is working on projects to maintain soccer excitement, particularly for youth leagues.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry notes overlapping events and asks about youth soccer legacy

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And I did forget one other event because we talked about we were trying to figure out what we can attribute to World Cup.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: We had the World Cup starting the 11th, the parade on the 18th, 250th anniversary, and the three-day Jay-Z concert.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So there was a lot happening in July in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So really looking forward to those numbers.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I have a question from Councilmember Gutierrez.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Is the city working on any projects to maintain the excitement around soccer, particularly for youth leagues?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Many were so involved in the festivities and watch parties.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Plus, we have a new stadium in my district, no doubt.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Feels like maybe the World Cup czar can become the soccer czar for the city.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And I know you still, or just our sports czar in general.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: What are you doing, Maya?

chapters.summary: Honda says the city was thrilled by the unexpected outpouring of excitement around soccer. She says the city is continuing conversations with council members about investment and channeling that excitement.
chapters.title: Honda says city continuing soccer excitement conversations

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: Career change, for sure.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: It's a great.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: question and I think we were overwhelmed, excited and thrilled by the, honestly, at sometimes unexpected outpouring of excitement around soccer, though it should have been expected, honestly, if we're being honest.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: So the answer is yes, we're continuing to have conversations, would love to also continue to have conversations with council members around what investment can look like and how we can channel that excitement.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Excellent.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks how and when SBS notified affected Midtown businesses about truck delivery restrictions. Gross says DOT managed the closures and SBS spoke to BIDs, chambers, merchants associations, and commissaries two weeks ahead of time.
chapters.title: SBS describes notification to businesses on Midtown truck restrictions

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: The city restricted, this is an SBS question, the city restricted truck deliveries in Midtown on all eight match days, and some Midtown businesses reported being unaware of the restrictions shortly before the tournament began.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: How and when did SBS notify affected businesses, and did SBS receive complaints about missed deliveries, and how were those addressed?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: So DOT, as they were managing all of the competing logistical needs of the city, determined to proceed, and the administration determined to proceed with closures.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: And in the planning of the decision on the closures, we were involved in determining

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: who would be reaching out to which stakeholders, and SBS was on the ground.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: We spoke to our business improvement district partners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: DOT spoke to them as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: We spoke to chambers, merchants associations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: And SBS, we thought to also ensure that street vendors are not impacted by these delivery restrictions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: So what we did is the truck deliveries,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: or not coming to the vendors themselves, but they go to commissaries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: And we intentionally made sure every single commissary in the impacted area ahead of time, two weeks ahead of time, was aware of the restrictions that they were going to be faced so that vendors could plan for that impact in their street vending operations.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks whether NYC Tourism will use a more tech-related program for future outreach. Mamana says the next time the city should set up a centralized dashboard to see participation in real time and start earlier.
chapters.title: Mamana proposes centralized dashboard for future business outreach

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And it was mentioned that most of the, this is for NYC tourism businesses, there was like a manual outreach for the future.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Do we plan on like coordinating or a program more tech related to kind of help alleviate some of that?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Do you mean for the CUP program?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: I think this was the first time that we reached out beyond our member base to virtually any outlet that served a cold beverage was eligible for this program.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: So it could have been street carts, bodegas.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: So we really did rely on associations, bids, and chambers to help get the word out beyond our purview.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: I think the next time we do this, we would just definitely set up a centralized dashboard so we could see in real time to the earlier point.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: And then we would ideally start earlier so that we can make up shortfalls as we see them with enough time.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Is there a way for SBS to coordinate with NYC Tourism to the businesses that are?

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: We did, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana
utterances.text: I think we just ran out of time.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Now, you heard.

chapters.summary: Gross says SBS targeted neighborhoods with high concentrations of immigrant-owned businesses. She says SBS wanted to engage cultural capitals and also support communities facing a perceived slowdown from federal immigration enforcement.
chapters.title: Gross explains targeted outreach to immigrant business communities

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: Chair, could I just add, without the dashboard, we made sure we were in neighborhoods with high concentrations of immigrant-owned businesses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: We were really trying to think of two goals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: One, all the cultural capitals of immigrant communities in New York City that were mobilized and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: enthusiastic about the World Cup, so making sure those folks who we knew naturally were planning on watch parties to celebrate their countries and communities were engaged and knew of how to get onto tourism's calendar, how to get onto the host committee's welcome rewards program,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: and all of those other services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: And the other goal here was we know there was a very real perceived slowdown in many immigrant communities following.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: the non-local law enforcement activities across the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: And so we also then targeted and made sure that the same immigrant communities that faced some slowdown because of federal threats were the same communities that were benefiting from the activities of the World Cup.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dynishal Gross
utterances.text: That's where, without any dashboard, we were deploying all of our outreach resources.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I appreciate it.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks how many applications for events during the tournament window were denied and how many denials were due to World Cup events. Honda says the summer was unprecedented and the city will come back with specific data.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry asks how many event permits were denied

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Now, we've heard a lot about the issues with permitting.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: At the end of the day, were we able to get a sense of how many applications for events during the tournament window were ultimately denied?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And of those denials, which were specifically attributed to World Cup events versus traditional, as my colleagues mentioned, block parties or other annual events that communities...

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Put together?

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: We will, it was an unprecedented summer, so we'll have to get you, we'll have to come back to you with the data on the specifics around this summer.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: I'll note that annual events were prioritized.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And so, you know, speaking in the general sense, typical block parties, any kind of summer celebration that usually occurs, we made every effort to make sure that it could go forward and was not affected by the World Cup.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks which agencies were designated to implement Local Laws 107 and 110 on cultural passports, maps, and public bathrooms. Honda says she cannot speak to specific agencies but highlights the cultural passport and digital map collaboration.
chapters.title: Honda discusses implementation of cultural passport and digital map laws

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Local laws 106, 107, and 110 of 2026 became law without the mayor's signature on June 13th, two days after the tournament began.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Which agencies were designated to implement local laws 107 and 110?

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: Were these the cultural passport and the map related?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: They were around the cultural passport, the map, and public bathroom expansion.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: I can't speak to the specifics of the agencies.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: I'm not sure if anyone else here can, but we can get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: I will note that we were thrilled to be able to put forward a cultural passport in the opening days of the World Cup.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: And that was an amazing collaboration that enabled folks, residents and visitors, to go to the public library and get a cultural passport and then use it to collect stamps made by New York City-based artists throughout the city.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: I know that public restroom expansion is in the works in partnership in some cases with city council and EDC is also doing some work there

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: and then we were very very excited to work with NYC tourism and the FIFA host committee on the digital map

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: and calendar and we also were able to do coordinated marketing efforts and I really want to speak to that coordination where

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: there was a scenario a terrible scenario in which everyone and their mother had a new map right and a different calendar and then no one knew where to go and half of them had these

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: events and half of them had those.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda

utterances.speaker: Nancy Mamana

utterances.text: I actually really want to commend the host committee, New York, New Jersey.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda
utterances.text: I think, you know, we all have seen the headlines of events at MetLife and what they can and have looked like in the past in terms of our ability to get people from here to there.

utterances.speaker: Maya Honda

chapters.summary: Alex Lasry introduces himself as CEO of the FIFA World Cup 2026 New York New Jersey Host Committee. He says the local organizing committee coordinated with FIFA, government agencies, transportation, public safety, private sector, and community organizations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chairs Maloney and Thomas Henry, members of the Committee on Economic Development and Small Business, and members of the Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: Thank you for this opportunity to be here today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: I'm Alex Lazary, and I serve as the CEO of the FIFA World Cup 2026 New York, New Jersey Host Committee, the local organizing committee responsible for coordinating with FIFA,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: government agencies, transportation, public safety partners, the private sector, and community organizations to plan and deliver our region's responsibilities as a host of the 2026 FIFA World Cup.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: to lead this organization and a team that spent years preparing New York and New Jersey to welcome the world.

chapters.summary: Lasry says the World Cup was a tremendous success by every major measure and generated an estimated $3.5 billion in regional economic impact. He says the work was guided by safety and security, transportation, fan experience, and economic impact.
chapters.title: Lasry outlines host committee success and four pillars

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: By every major measure we established going into the tournament, the World Cup was a tremendous success for New York and New Jersey.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: We safely welcomed hundreds of thousands of match attendees and millions of visitors and fans across the region.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: We moved unprecedented crowds through one of the most complex transportation networks in the world.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: And we created free opportunities for New Yorkers to experience the tournament across all five boroughs and generated an estimated $3.5 billion in regional economic impact, exceeding our original projections.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: And those outcomes reflected the four key pillars that guided our work from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: Safety and security, transportation, fan experience, and economic impact.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: Our goal was to deliver across all four while demonstrating once again why New York is the best city in the world to host the biggest global sporting events in the world.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: New York is no stranger to mega events.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: This is a city that routinely welcomes the world for major sporting events, concerts, cultural celebrations, and global gatherings, while continuing to serve more than 8 million New Yorkers every day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: But events of the scale of the World Cup do not succeed simply because they come to New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: They require years of planning, coordination, and investment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: And that is why our four pillars were fundamentally connected.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: A safe, reliable, and welcoming tournament experience was essential to bringing visitors here, moving them throughout the region, and ultimately realizing the extraordinary economic opportunity that came with hosting the world's largest sporting event.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: York and New Jersey approached that responsibility as one region.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: We bid together, planned together, and ultimately delivered eight matches, including the final, as a single destination.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: That required years of coordination among federal, state, and local governments, law enforcement agencies, transportation authorities, venue operators, FIFA, and the private sector.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: The results demonstrated the strength of that collaboration.

chapters.summary: Lasry says more than 645,000 fans attended eight matches and about 98% entered before kickoff. He says the stadium property was cleared in under two and a half hours, beating the pre-tournament goal of three hours.
chapters.title: Lasry reports match attendance and transportation outcomes

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: More than 645,000 fans attended our eight matches.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: Approximately 98% of the spectators entered the stadium before kickoff across the tournament.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: And following the matches, we cleared the stadium property in under two and a half hours, beating our pre-tournament goal of three hours.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: At the same time, our transportation network continued to serve the millions of residents who rely on it every day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: But while the matches were an important part of our work, what makes the World Cup special is everything that happens beyond the stadium.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: We hosted eight matches, but the World Cup lasted 39 days.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: We wanted the experience throughout those 39 days to rival what was happening on the pitch.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: And we wanted visitors from around the world and New Yorkers alike to have the opportunity to be a part of it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: We wanted the world to know that if you want to have the biggest stars on the biggest stage, you want to be in New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: We wanted to prove that New York is still the world's capital for sports, entertainment, and tourism.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: That meant thinking differently about how the World Cup could show up across the city.

chapters.summary: Lasry says the original plan was a single fan fest at Liberty State Park, but the host committee created a distributed network of fan experiences. He says it facilitated more than 180 public viewing licenses and over 5,000 young people participated in soccer programming.
chapters.title: Lasry describes distributed fan fests and community soccer programs

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: Our original planning contemplated a single centralized fan fest at Liberty State Park.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: But as our plans evolved, we saw an opportunity to create something broader, a distributed network of fan experiences across New York and New Jersey.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: In the city, that meant free public fan experiences across all five boroughs, bringing the tournament directly into communities and allowing New Yorkers to participate regardless of whether they held a match ticket.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: We also wanted to harness the creative energy that is unique to New York and give communities the ability to create their own World Cup experiences.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: We pursued a bottom-up strategy, helping facilitate more than 180 public viewing licenses across all five boroughs, so restaurants, bars, and community venues could host watch parties and become part of the tournament.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: We worked with organizations including the YMCA of Greater New York City, in the community, South Bronx United, Street Soccer USA, Gotham FC, NYC FC, and the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: Soccer Foundation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: Across the region, more than 5,000 young people participated directly in clinics, pitch days, tournaments, and other community programming.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: And we also expanded access to matches for community members, including New York City public school soccer players and hospitality workers who helped welcome visitors throughout the tournament.

chapters.summary: Lasry says the host committee contracted with over 100 New York City vendors and spent more than $10 million with New York City-based businesses, including 36 MWBEs. He also describes the World Cup concierge and Welcome World Rewards program.
chapters.title: Lasry details $10M with NYC vendors and 36 MWBEs

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: That same philosophy informed our approach to small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: The host committee contracted with over 100 New York City vendors and spent more than $10 million with New York City-based businesses, including 36 MWBEs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: Rather than create programs in isolation, we work to amplify existing city initiatives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: We integrated New York City tourism and conventions, five borough winners special, into our World Cup concierge and welcome awards program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: The concierge developed with Google Gemini and Google Maps encourage visitors to explore neighborhood destinations, community events, and ethnic enclaves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: throughout the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: Welcome World Rewards created another direct connection to local businesses with more than 1,000 participating businesses and destinations across the region, leading to over 10,000 small business visits from locals and visitors alike.

chapters.summary: Lasry says the World Cup generated $3.5 billion in regional economic impact, including $2 billion for New York City, $1.9 billion in direct spending, 27,000 jobs, and $414 million in state and local tax revenue. He says the host committee invested in permanent mini pitches in the Bronx, Brooklyn, Queens, and Staten Island.
chapters.title: Lasry reports $3.5B regional impact and permanent soccer investments

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: We also wanted part of this investment to remain long after the tournament ended.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: Working with the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: Soccer Foundation and other partners, we invested in permanent mini pitches and soccer infrastructure, including projects in the Bronx, Brooklyn, Queens, and Staten Island.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: Taken together, these efforts contributed to an extraordinary result.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: The World Cup generated an estimated $3.5 billion in total economic impact across the region, $2 billion of which were for New York City, exceeding our original projections.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: That included $1.9 billion in direct spending, more than 27,000 jobs supported, $1.4 billion in labor income, and more than $414 million in state and local tax revenue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: Every investment required to deliver our joint bid contributed to that success, from the operations necessary to stage the matches and move hundreds of thousands of people to free fan experiences, local business programs, and community investments throughout New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: The World Cup was a huge success for the region, but its significance extends beyond what we accomplished over those 39 days.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: It demonstrated that New York and New Jersey can successfully deliver an event of extraordinary global scale while creating meaningful opportunities for the people, businesses, and communities that call this region home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: New York has always been where the world comes for its biggest moments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: The World Cup reaffirmed that we remain the best city in the world for major sports.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: and entertainment events, and provided a model for how we can approach the many global events that will come here next.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: We're incredibly proud of what we accomplished together and of the opportunities the World Cup created for New Yorkers across all five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: Thank you, and happy to take any questions.

chapters.summary: Maloney welcomes Lasry to his first City Council hearing and asks for a breakdown of expenditures from the $20 million EDC contract. Lasry says the vast majority was spent on free fan festivals after the host committee pivoted from Liberty State Park.
chapters.title: Maloney asks Lasry for breakdown of $20M EDC contract

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you for being here and congratulations on your first hearing with the City Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: Go easy on me.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: One of the things that we were asking a lot of questions about before is a breakdown of the expenditures for the $20 million under contract with EDC and if you have any details on how that money was allocated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: So the vast majority of the money spent from EDC was on the free fan festivals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: So when we pivoted from Liberty State Park to bringing the Fan Fest to New York, we really saw this as an opportunity to...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: really, I think, do what we thought, which was make New York City, you know, kind of the center of these experiences outside of the stadium.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: And working with the mayor's office and creating free fan experiences all throughout New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: As I said, what we were really hoping to do was

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: create an experience outside of the stadium that would rival what was happening inside.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: We knew that, again, the stadium's only going to fit 80,000 people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: So only, but the stadium's going to fit 80,000 people, whether it's a World Cup, a Taylor Swift concert, a Super Bowl.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: It's going to be the same amount of people no matter what.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: What makes the World Cup so unique are the millions of people that come, not really ever expecting to get inside the tournament.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: And what we wanted to do was make sure that we were providing accessible and affordable spaces for people to participate in what is the world's largest sporting event.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: And what makes New York so unique are the spaces that it has.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: And so working with the city to make sure that we were able to kind of show off the crown jewels of the city in every neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: And I think we really wanted to make sure that we weren't just focused on Manhattan, but making sure that we were directing people to Staten Island, the Bronx, Brooklyn and Queens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: And when you look at, I think, the biggest fan fest that we put on at the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: Tennis Center, bringing people to the, you know, one of the biggest and well-known global international destinations for sports,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: bringing people to the Bronx at Bronx Terminal Market, going to Brooklyn for the Adidas Fan Fest at Brooklyn Bridge Park, and then also at Staten Island at the ballpark doing a four-day fan festival there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: So really trying to broaden an experience, and that was what a vast majority of the funds were used for.

chapters.summary: Maloney asks how the fan initiatives translated into economic impact. Lasry says the host committee did a regional economic impact report and did not break it down by city or state, relying on the city and NYC Tourism for city-specific analysis.
chapters.title: Lasry says host committee did not break down impact by city

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And from those initiatives, do you know how that translated into real economic impact?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And if you have those estimates or anything you could share.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: So as a regional bid committee, we did a regional economic impact and didn't break anything down by city or state.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: We were very intentional about the fact that, again, for us being the New York, New Jersey host committee, we really viewed this as a strong New Jersey was going to lead to a strong New York and a strong New York was going to lead to a stronger New Jersey.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: And so for us, our economic impact report really was a regional impact report.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: I would probably rely on the city and NYC Tourism and whoever else to put together a city-specific economic impact.

chapters.summary: Maloney asks whether there will be any follow-up analysis or details. Lasry says the host committee will not do a city-specific analysis but can provide fan fest attendance numbers, including over one million at Rockefeller Center and 200,000 at the U.S. Tennis Center.
chapters.title: Maloney presses for city-specific follow-up analysis

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So there won't be any follow-up analysis or details?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: We won't do a city-specific, because, again, as a regional committee, I think what we can see is the amount of people that we saw at the New York City Fan Festivals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: So for us, what we saw, and I can get the...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: The amount of people that we had at the fan fests.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: I do know that at Rock Center specific, there were over a million people that went to the Fan Village at Rock Center.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: In my district.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: It was, you know, kind of, again, one of the crown jewels.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: I know we had 50,000 plus people at Central Park.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: I think over 200,000 people at the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: Tennis Center for Queens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: You know, Brooklyn, I think, again, also over, I think, 200,000 people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: Bronx and Staten Island, I believe for those were in the 20 plus thousand people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: So New York City, again, for the fan festivals outside of the stadium, a real, real big impact.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: And it's, you know, again, I think always with this is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: We tried to blend into what was going on with the city, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: And that's what makes New York unique.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: It's also hard for us to measure the impact of the over 100, you know, the 180 viewing licenses that we help secure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: I think that was the most of any host city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: Just, again, trying to make sure that the entire region for whoever wanted to put on a watch party was able to.

chapters.summary: Maloney asks whether FIFA or the host committee provided resources for security or NYPD overtime. Lasry says the host committee worked with the federal government and received upwards of $60 million in federal reimbursements split across New York and New Jersey.
chapters.title: Maloney asks about security funding and federal reimbursements

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And did...

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: If any of them.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I think you heard my question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: Did we share them with who?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: The question is, did FIFA or the host committee provide any resources or financial support for security at events, for NYPD overages that the city had, or attendees that were traveling to and from the events?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: If you can speak a bit to the partnership there in financing the additional operational costs that came to both municipalities, but mainly I'm interested in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: So we actually worked with the federal government on securing federal reimbursements for security for the World Cup.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: So overtime funding, we were able to receive upwards of $60-plus million in federal reimbursements that we split across New York and New Jersey.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: We are in the process of taking in all of the submissions right now and then making sure that those reimbursements get set up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: So there was a $625 million aid package that was sent, that was signed, that was passed by Congress and signed by the.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: president for the World Cup split across the all the host cities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: We took again what were our best projections at the time and submitting for for those for the potential reimbursements and we believe that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: You know, we are now taking in all the submissions, so there will be federal support and reimbursements for some of the security overtime overages that should help cover the World Cup costs.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And that is roughly $30 million or so or a little more than that?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: We're still taking in all of the submissions, so I can get back to you on how the split worked.

chapters.summary: Maloney asks who had access to the contract between the host committee or FIFA and the city. Lasry says the contract was negotiated by the previous administrations in New Jersey and New York City and he would leave sharing it up to the city.
chapters.title: Maloney asks whether host committee can share FIFA contract

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Who had access to the contract between the host committee or FIFA in the city?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: That was before I started, but I believe the contract was done through the, I believe, the previous administration

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: in both New Jersey and New York City and was negotiated between those two administrations and FIFA as there was.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: I don't believe a host committee set up before the bid was awarded.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And have you seen the contract, the details of the contract?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, I've seen the contract.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And is that something you can share with the city council and the taxpayers?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: I would probably leave that up to the city as it's...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: Their contract.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Was there any

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Anything unique in that contract to New York?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: I don't think nothing that wasn't responsible for New Jersey as well.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Or relative to other cities that were hosting FIFA?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: All right, passing to my chair.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks how revenue from local and corporate funding was shared between FIFA and New York City. Lasry says any funding the host committee raised went to the host committee and into World Cup operations.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry questions host committee fundraising and budget

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So first question, as part of the chair of the host committee, one of the responsibilities is securing local and corporate funding for events.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Sorry, what was that?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Securing local and corporate funding for the events throughout the city.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: How was that revenue shared between FIFA and the city of New York?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Any sponsorships?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: Any funding that we raised went to the host committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: FIFA did their own fundraising.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So anything went to the host committee and then...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: Any corporate sponsorships that we personally raised for went to us.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And then where does that money go?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: So that went into operations as well for the World Cup.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: So we had a...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: We had a budget that we had to raise for.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: So we would go to corporate partners to try to raise to help fill the budget gaps.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks for the host committee's total budget. Lasry says it was upwards of $200 million, and Thomas-Henry asks how much was spent with local businesses and MWBEs.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry asks about $200M budget and local business spending

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: What was the total budget?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: We were upwards of $200 million.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And of that $200 million,

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: $100 million, $10 million was spent with local businesses?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: No, more than that was spent with local businesses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: But again, we had to go across New York and New Jersey.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Do you have an idea of what that small business or local business spend was?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: I can get that for you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And do you know, and of that number was roughly 30% of that to MWBEs?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: I mean, it's a little bit more, I don't think it's as simple as looking at how that broke out because for a lot of these mega events and kind of the big watch parties that we're putting on,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: one, we didn't produce a lot of them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: So we would hire a production company.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: So for Central Park, Global Citizen would put that on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: So it's a little bit more difficult for us to break out exactly how the percentages of spend there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: Also, there are only so many companies that can actually put on some of those watch parties and have the resources to be able to do that in such a tight time frame.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: With that being said, I don't have the percent breakdown of what was spent with MWBs.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks whether contracts required local or MWBE spending and what goods or services were procured. Lasry says any money given by New York was spent in New York City, but production companies often handled watch parties.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry asks how host committee procured from local and MWBE businesses

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Did we require any type of local spending or MWBE spending within those contracts?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: We made sure any money that was given to us by New York was spent in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And how did you go about procuring, what types of goods or services were procured by the local businesses in the city?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: I mean, those would have been for any of the watch parties that we put on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: So making sure that...

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Like production equipment and...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: You know, vendors at any of the watch parties.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: But again, for us, and I think it's important to note, we really wanted to make sure that the host committee wasn't going to be...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: The main source of wasn't going to be the only source or even the main source of economic impact, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: That is not what the host committees as a as a spender was.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: What we really wanted to do was plug into what was going into the city and amplify all of what the city was already doing to make sure that people who were coming here knew exactly where to go.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: So it wasn't going to be, hey, we are throwing this one big watch party.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: We want as much as we wanted as many people to come as possible, and they did.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: We also wanted people to explore the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: So you would come to our event in Queens, but then we really wanted you to go to bars, restaurants, et cetera, in the neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: And that was where we saw the real big economic impact.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks how the host committee collaborated with NYC Tourism and collected data on driving traffic to local businesses. Lasry says the host committee was small and did its best, promoting fan zones and local watch parties.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry asks how host committee measured traffic to local businesses

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: How was the data you guys saw in terms of driving traffic to the local businesses in comparison to NYC tourism?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Was it the same data or did you?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And how did you collaborate with NYC tourism in terms of getting folks from the fan clubs to?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: the local businesses and how did you collect that data?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Is this same data?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: We tried our best to collect the data as best we could, but we were a small but mighty team that had a lot that we had to do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: And we didn't have a team of 100 people that could also go and do data collection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: So we did the best that we could.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: I can't speak to NYC Tourism, although I know that they were an incredible partner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: And for us, though, what we tried to do was if you were at our fan zones or at any of our fan fest, we tried to promote the ability for people to then go outside

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: and go outside of just the fan zone that they were in and go experience other spots.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: If there were people who were throwing their own watch parties through our viewing license or anything, we tried to promote that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: Any of the advertising that the city or New York City tourism was doing, we tried to promote that as well.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks how the host committee identified local businesses and MWBEs for procurement. Lasry says it hired a consultant, Tiffany Stenard, to help monitor and procure MWBEs, but much work went through large production agencies.
chapters.title: Lasry says consultant helped monitor MWBE procurement

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And what tools and methods?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alex Lasry
utterances.text: I've got to, sorry, just because we started a little late, I'm going to have only like a couple more minutes.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
